utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: If your Honour pleases, my name is Grant Niemann. I appear with Mr. Akhavan for the Respondent.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. BABIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, my name is Jovan Babic, attorney from Yugoslavia, defence counsel for the accused, Mr. Erdemovic. PRESIDENT CASSESE: Mr. Erdemovic, can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: MR. ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, your Honours. PRESIDENT CASSESE: Thank you. Well, this morning we will concentrate our hearing on the preliminary issues which were set out in the scheduling order we issued on 5th May 1997, and in this connection I should like to thank both parties for promptly complying with the request for submission of written briefs, a request contained in that order. Before we start, may I also add that the appeals chamber has decided not to grant leave to file an amicus curiae brief to Mr. Sienho Yee. Let me tell you now how we intend to proceed. Since both parties have submitted exhaustive written briefs, I think they should not restate their position here. I will ask each of them whether they want to add anything, in which case each party will have ten minutes available. After that, the court will ask questions so as better to clarify the views of each party. If this is agreeable to you, I will start by asking defence counsel whether he has anything to add to his brief, again solely with regard to the preliminary issues we judges raised in our order of 5th May. Mr. Babic?

utterances.speaker: MR. BABIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I think that in my brief I was clear regarding my positions, which range from the closing statement to the appeal, the argument for the appeal and the motion on preliminary issues, and I really have nothing more to add to those briefs. PRESIDENT CASSESE: Thank you. May I therefore turn to the prosecutor and ask him whether he has anything to add to his written brief?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: We have, your Honours. Your Honours, we have prepared a fairly substantial submission, in fact, to assist the court, particularly on the question of how we say international law deals with this topic, and we have in that endeavoured to deal with the authorities and to argue how those authorities would lead to an inevitable conclusion, that duress is not available in a crime that involves the killing of innocent human beings. We have also dealt with various aspects of the transcript which we considered would assist the court in looking at the way this matter progressed through the court into the sentencing court. It seems, your Honour, that if you wish us to deal with it in ten minutes, we are not going to be able to do it in that time. I understand that the submissions on international law are in a fairly complete state, and if it would assist the court we could hand up a copy of that, but we would be anxious to put to the court, because we consider it a complex issue, complex for two reasons: one, because there is a division in the various jurisdictions of the world, a division particularly between civil law and Common Law, and we say that that leads to an inconclusive position, and with the international law we argue that it is clear, but it is not clear on a prima facie glance at it, because there has been an influence of, we would say, the civil law position on the international law, but at the end of the day we would argue that the authority clearly points to the conclusion that duress is not available. We are anxious to present that to the appeal court. If your Honour would prefer, we can do it by way of handing up a written submission. I should add, your Honour, that it was prepared for the purposes of an oral address, so it will have the defects about it which would suggest that it was prepared for that purpose alone, but save and except that, if your Honour wishes to merely deal very briefly with the matter, I would ask the court's leave to tender that. PRESIDENT CASSESE: Well, may I ask you how much time you would need now to add your remarks?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. Your Honours, the issue of international law, my colleague was going to deal with that. If I may confer with him for a moment. Your Honour, if I may be permitted to speak for ten minutes and if Mr. Akhavan could speak for that same period of time, I think we could dispose of it in that period of time, if that would be permissible. PRESIDENT CASSESE: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honours, in our submission in answer to the first question we would argue that clearly whether duress is a defence to a crime against humanity or war crime, when the underlying offence is the killing of innocent human beings, is clearly low. Apart from the international law issues that will be examined by my colleague, Mr. Akhavan, momentarily, we say the position is also interesting in the United Kingdom. For instance, in 1975 there was a case that came before the House of Lords of Lynch v the Director of Public Prosecutions for Northern Ireland, which was reported in 1975, 1 All England Reports at page 913. In that their Lords considered the possibility of introducing a defence of duress in cases of attempted murder as opposed to murder in the first degree. This case was then very quickly reconsidered by the House in a case of Abbott V Queen, reported in 1976, 3 All England Reports, page 140. This was where the House sat as the Privy Council. In that decision Lord Salmon made a very instructive and important speech, in our submission, on the issue of duress, when the underlying offence involves the killing of an innocent human being. In particular His Honour looked at -- his Lordship looked at the position from the point of view of war crimes cases that occurred during the second world war, and in his speech he addressed it from that point of view and concluded that it would be most unfortunate if the Common Law of England was to be varied or changed so as to admit duress in circumstances where it involved in that case murder in the first degree. So even though there was a momentary shift towards the possibility of admitting duress in Lynch v DPP, one year later it changed back very dramatically, and ultimately, your Honours, in 1987, in the case of Howe reported in 1987, 1 All England Reports at page 771, the House of Lords overruled Lynch's case. So, in our submission, that is an interesting experience in the development of the law. Your Honours, in our submission there will always be cases that arouses the sympathy of the court because of the circumstances under which the crime was committed. However, the solution to the problem is not to permit duress to be a defence to a crime where the underlying offence involves the killing of innocent human beings, but to mitigate the penalty. To the extent to which the court is moved to be merciful mitigation, in our submission, can be as broad as the sentencing discretion of the court itself and in appropriate circumstances can legitimately amount to no prison sentence being imposed at all, but the life of innocent human beings murdered by a principal of the first degree cannot be rendered so cheap as to justify the approbation of the court, in our submission. Your Honours, moving on to the next question: was the guilty plea entered by the Defendant at the initial appearance equivocal? In our submission it was not equivocal. The accused unequivocally pleaded guilty to the crime and after pleading guilty he merely raised an excuse by way of mitigation. That was that he had acted under superior orders, which orders he felt obliged to obey. Lest there be any uncertainty about that, the presiding judge was very careful in ensuring that he clarified the matter, and at page 9 of the transcript of 31st May 1996 at line 11 through to 12 your Honours can see where His Honour Judge Jorda dealt with this question when it was raised. In our submission, your Honour, the initial position that was adopted by the accused did not change with the passage of time, because six months later, when he was before the chamber on 19th November, at page 36 of the transcript, lines 1-3, the position he adopted was the same. Dealing with the plea of guilty itself, your Honours, in our submission the presiding judge dealt with this matter with great care and detail. When he was dealing with the plea of guilty he dealt with Article 21, paragraph 4A of the Statute of the Tribunal, ensuring that the accused understood the charges. He also went to detailed length to ensure that the accused had the opportunity to prepare, that he would be given a fair and public hearing, that his right to be heard would be respected and that he understood the sentence with which he was faced, and primarily that he knew what he was doing by reason of the plea. Now, your Honours, in our submission at no initial stage -- at no stage of the initial appearance did counsel for the accused raise the issue of duress. Clearly the idea of raising duress had not occurred to counsel for defence at that stage of the proceedings. It was only during the course of the final address some six months later did we hear the matter raised by defence counsel for the first time, and when he does raise it, it is different to the basis of what the Defendant raised when he raised it with the sentencing judge. The problem with this is that the question of the accused's mental state and the need for psychiatric analysis was, as I say, not raised by the accused. Initially it was brought up by the chamber itself, who sought this psychiatric analysis in order to assist it with sentencing. Even when it was brought up, in our submission at that stage it was not discussed in any detail by counsel for the accused or the accused himself. When the report came before the court, again the issue of his state of mind at the time of the commission of the offence was not raised. So in our submission, your Honours, this was all something that came up quite belatedly and we would suggest opportunistically. Your Honours, in our submission, if counsel for the accused generally held any concerns for the state of the accused's mental condition at the time of the commission of the crime rather than just raising it during the course of his closing address, then he had ample opportunity to do something about that. He had seven months, in our submission, from the time when the decision for him to come to The Hague and finally he was heard in order to go out and obtain any necessary reports which he may have felt would assist him. Finally, your Honour, there was a suggestion at some stage during the proceedings in the sentencing court where the accused suggested that he was subsequently shot because he had not obeyed the superior orders that he was given. We submit, your Honours, that there is no basis to that. We say there is no basis to it because, firstly, he disobeyed superior orders on a previous occasion and there was no consequence that flowed from that; secondly, he disobeyed superior orders on a subsequent occasion to the one in question and there was no serious consequences flowed from that; and ultimately, your Honours, the persons responsible presumably inflicting this injury upon him then subsequently turned around and arranged for his transfer to Belgrade where he received medical treatment, which we would suggest is somewhat inconsistent with the sanction of being shot being imposed on him for failure to obey the orders. Finally, when he goes to Belgrade investigators from Republika Srpska and Bjelova come over to investigate the offence. Ultimately there is some hearing before a court on this matter, where one of the witnesses at least says it all occurred in circumstances where they were in a bar, they were drunk and one soldier shot upon another. In those circumstances we submit that there is no basis whatsoever to suggest that he was genuinely under fear of being shot as a consequence of not complying with a superior order that he was given. We add to that the fact that he had done it before. He had disobeyed orders before. So presumably if he genuinely feared for his wife and child, then he did not fear for them on those other occasions. It was only on this occasion with which he has been charged that he was concerned. Finally, your Honours, was acceptance of the guilty plea valid at the time of his initial appearance in view of his mental condition or was any defect in the proceedings corrected by his statements at subsequent proceedings? Your Honours, I need go no further, I think, than to say that even the accused himself in his brief says that he maintains his position with respect to his plea of guilty and in our submission an examination of the transcript clearly demonstrates at no stage has he moved from that position. He clearly says he is guilty of an offence. He has said so. On numerous occasions he has been questioned about it, but he maintains that. In any event and in conclusion, once a plea of guilty has been entered, once a person has been sentenced, then even if there is equivocation, then in our submission that is not a basis upon which to set aside the plea. There is authority in support of that proposition and the authority on which I rely primarily is a decision of North Carolina V Alfred. It is reported in 400 US reports, page 25, but also there is the case of R v Sullivan, 1984, 2 All England Reports at page 673. In this case the House did not actually deal with that specific issue, but it dealt with the situation where a person, clearly innocent, had pleaded guilty in circumstances where he would have faced the alternative of being found insane and the House of Lords found no difficulty in the plea being accepted in those circumstances. Thank you, your Honours. PRESIDENT CASSESE: Thank you. Mr. Akhavan?

utterances.speaker: MR. AKHAVAN
utterances.text: Honourable Members of the Chamber, in the limited time that is available to me I would like to quickly summarise the main points of the Prosecutor's argument on the question of whether duress can ever be admissible as a defence to the crime of killing an innocent human being. By way of introduction I simply want to emphasise that duress is an excuse under the law and not a justification. It is often said that duress is such that the actions of the accused are not voluntary. However, duress does not concern itself with the situation in which a person is compelled by physical force to go through the motions of an actus reus without any choice on his or her part. In such cases the accused would be invariably exculpated. He would not be guilty of any blameworthy conduct on the fundamental ground that he did not exercise choice, that he did not act, but as an excuse duress does not pre-suppose that the accused did not have mens rea. As the English law commentators Smith and Hogan observe, when duress is invoked as an defence the accused admits that he was able to control his action, and chose to do the act with which he is charged but denies responsibility for doing so. He may say: "I had no choice", but that is not strictly true. The alternative to committing the crime may have been so exceedingly unattractive that no reasonable person would have chosen it, but there was a choice". Duress, therefore, your Honours, I would submit is not -- PRESIDENT CASSESE: Sorry, Mr. Babic?

utterances.speaker: MR. BABIC
utterances.text: I do not hear the translator. PRESIDENT CASSESE: There is a problem with translation, I understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. BABIC
utterances.text: Okay. PRESIDENT CASSESE: Thank you. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. AKHAVAN
utterances.text: Therefore, your Honours, duress is not a categorical defence to criminal conduct, because unlike other defences it does not pre-suppose an absence of mens rea. The notion that an act committed under duress is involuntary is simply a legal fiction, as described by the Supreme Court of Canada in the 1984 case of Perka v The Queen, reported in 1984, 13 Dominion Law Reports, 4th series at 1. As described by the Supreme Court the involuntary aspect of duress is simply "measured on the basis of society's expectation of appropriate and normal resistance to pressure". Therefore, I wish simply to emphasise that unlike justifications, duress is an excuse and its scope is determined, as the Supreme Court of Canada said, based on societal expectations. It would not violate any fundamental principle of criminal law if the appeals chamber was to choose not to apply it to the crime of murder. Moving on quickly, your Honours, to the question of duress as a defence to murder under international law, as our written submission clearly indicates, the overwhelming weight of evidence in the post second world war decisions indicates categorically that duress can never be admitted as a defence to the crime of murder. As indicated, the only exception, the only clear exception to this rule, is the Einsatzgruppen trial before the US Military Tribunal. However, as pointed out in our submission, that case does not cite any authority whatsoever in support of its proposition that duress can be a defence to murder, and the case indeed goes against the law of the United States military courts as well as the Anglo-American Common Law, and as further pointed out, this decision has strongly been criticised by leading commentators, including Professor Hersch Lauterpacht and Yoram Dinstein. I wish simply to emphasise also that the Common Law pedigree of international law in this respect should in no way put into question the position of international law on the admissibility of duress as a defence. Such an argument, the argument that the court must somehow reject the overwhelming weight of authority of this case law, simply because it has a Common Law orientation, would overlook the essentially eclectic character of international criminal law, borrowing, as it does, from various legal systems, often haphazardly. If the pedigree of each and every norm was to be examined and contested before this court, it would undermine the entire edifice of this body of law. To quickly give but one example, the law of conspiracy when it was discussed in 1944, during the preparatory work of the Nuremberg Charter, was considered by the French delegation, and I quote from Bradley Smith, a leading commentator, "as a barbarous concept unworthy of modern law". The Soviet delegation was outright shocked at the concept of conspiracy. Nevertheless it was retained in the charter and it was developed through the case law both of the international military Tribunal and the courts under control council law number 10. It cannot now be argued that conspiracy, because of its Common Law pedigree, should not be admitted as a concept under international criminal law. I would submit, your Honour, that the same clearly applies to the defence of duress. The fact that the position of international law concurs by virtue of historical or other circumstances with the Common Law position, the fact that duress clearly cannot be a defence to murder under international law, cannot be in any way challenged because of the pedigree or origins of that concept. I would end, your Honours, by emphasising that one cannot resolve this question of law through an exhaustive survey of all legal systems under the category of general principles of law. Firstly, the Nuremberg decisions themselves are recognised as a reflection of general principles of law. This is very clear from the preparatory work of the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights with respect to Article 15, paragraph 2, which recognises general principles as a means of satisfying the nullem crimen principle and which was specifically included to ratify the jurisprudence of the post-Second World War trials. The same applies to Article 7, paragraph 2 of the European Convention on Human Rights, and there is case law which clearly supports the proposition that the jurisprudence of these tribunals is a reflection of general principles. Secondly, to try to resolve such a highly specific question of law based on general principles would be exceedingly difficult. General principles by their very nature are general. They are not intended to be used for the determination of highly specific questions such as that before the court. In any event such an expedition would not result in a clear answer, because it is very clear that domestic legal systems have very different positions, and I may say these different positions are not simply between the Common Law and Civil Law systems, but in Common Law systems as well there is considerable divergence on the scope of duress as a defence. By way of example, in the United Kingdom, duress is a defence to all crimes with the exception of murder, aiding and abetting murder and the crime of treason, involving death of the Sovereign, but in Canada, in the criminal code of Canada, it is applied to a wide range of offences, meaning to say that duress cannot be a defence not only to murder or treason, but also to other acts, such as causing grave bodily harm, such as sexual assault, such as kidnapping. Therefore, the only way that this court can resolve this question with certainty is by looking at the relevant international law as decided by the courts following the Second World War, and that we submit clearly indicates on the overwhelming weight of authority that duress cannot be admitted as a full defence to the crime of murder. Unless I may be of further assistance, your Honour, those are the submissions of the Prosecutor. PRESIDENT CASSESE: Thank you very much indeed for being so concise. Before we start with questions, I would like to turn to the defence counsel to ask him whether he would like to comment on the oral submissions of the Prosecutor. Mr. Babic?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. BABIC
utterances.text: Just a few remarks, your Honours. We are dealing here with the relationship between the general and specific sections of criminal codes in countries in which the criminal law has been codified. Therefore, in the European codes, not in a single criminal code that I have had access to, and I have referred to them in my brief, not a single institution from the general part of the Criminal Code has been excluded in relation to any criminal offence in the specific part of the Criminal Code. Therefore, if an institution in the general section of the Criminal Code, such as extreme necessity, duress, self-defence, and all the other general institutions, are proven in the proceedings, then they can and must be applied in relation to all criminal acts regardless of its seriousness that is the basic premise of all the Criminal Codes of the European countries, in my submission. If we were not to accept this, then we would go back to the principle which we do not wish to question: "nemo crimen sine lege, nemo pene sine lege" (sic), which means we have no general institutions. In the initial hearings I said that my main problem was which law should be applied, Common Law, Anglo-Saxon law, Civil Law or some institutions such as the Nuremberg trials, case law and so on. That is as far as duress is concerned and the general institutions of criminal law. The Prosecutor submits that duress is determined on the basis of the expectations of society. Which society? If we are talking about the society in the territory of the former Yugoslavia and the moral position of that society in relation to such and similar offences, then the position of that society is expressed in the motto of my argument of the appeal, and that is to do evil by defending oneself against evil is no crime. That is the motto. It is not possible to exclude duress if it exists in relation to the classical act of murder. If it is proven in the proceedings, it must be accepted. When my learned colleague elaborates on this all, referring to authorities, he is actually always referring to national laws and national judicial decisions. So let us see. If we do not have a codified international criminal law, then we must see which national laws and which national judicial decisions are relevant. The last point I wish to make regarding the mental state. My learned colleagues incorrectly saying that the defence did not react in time regarding mental state. The defence did not have the chance, nor should it have commented on that, because the very guilty plea of the accused, when he explained the conditions under which the act was committed, that defence existed from the very first statement made by the accused before this trial chamber. Those would be my comments, your Honours. PRESIDENT CASSESE: Thank you. I suggest, if my colleagues are agreeable, now to start with questions to both parties, and I would like to start with questions to defence counsel. I have two questions relating to what you wrote in your written briefs as well as what you said this morning. My first question is as follows. In your written brief, Mr. Babic, you argue that Erdemovic acted under duress or, as you say, necessity. Necessity is a defence in that and I quote your words "it precludes either the existence of the offence or the Defendant's guilt". You also say that in Yugoslavia, and again I quote your words "a sharp distinction is made between a criminal offence and criminal responsibility". You go on to say: "The fact that someone has committed a criminal offence does not mean that he necessarily is criminally responsible". Now, this is in line with what you actually stated before the trial chamber in your closing argument, which I have with me, and there -- I am afraid I am quoting from the English version -- on page 57 you said, line 29: "In his statement Erdemovic actually incriminated himself and defended himself at the same time". Then on page 62 you quote quite a few criminal codes of various European countries, which all state, according to you, but I think there you are correct, that the existence of extreme necessity is a ground for the exclusion of illegality and guilt or exclusion of criminal responsibility. Consistent with this position on page 64 and 65 and of your transcript -- again I am quoting your closing argument -- you stated that you requested that your client, Mr. Erdemovic, be acquitted. Then as an alternative argument you requested that duress or necessity should be regarded as a mitigating circumstance. Now, if this is so, how can you then argue that the guilty plea does not have an ambiguous character? Again I am putting your words, the words in your written brief concerning the preliminary issue. In paragraph 2 you say: "The guilty plea does not have an ambiguous character". Do you not find contradict re or inconsistent to state on the one hand that the Defendant, although he committed an offence, is not criminally responsible because of necessity and then to state, on the other hand, that the guilty plea is valid? You know, Mr. Babic, under our Statute, as you know, to plead guilty is not the same as to confess to the perpetration of an offence. Under the Statute of our Tribunal to plead guilty means to admit to one's criminal responsibility. After pleading guilty there no longer arises the problem of whether or not one is criminally responsible. This problem of criminal responsibility is settled by the guilty plea. The only problem that arises at that point revolves around the penalty to be meted out, the sentence. I wonder whether you could comment on this remark I have just made, where to stress it again, I find a contradiction in your statement. Could you comment on that?

utterances.speaker: MR. BABIC
utterances.text: Honourable Mr. President, I fail to see any contradiction in my submissions, and having said this I find the grounds for saying this in the national legislation of my country, in its practice and judicial theory. According to the Criminal Code of Yugoslavia for someone to be sentenced and for someone to be found guilty it is necessary to prove the objective elements of the act and the subjective elements of the act. Let me make a small digression. In the proceedings that we had here I personally believe, although my honourable colleague the Prosecutor is reproaching me for this, that it was up to him to prove both the objective and subjective elements of offence for someone to be found guilty by this chamber. He is saying that I did not make a motion for experts to make an examination regarding the mental state of the accused at the time of the offence. It was the duty of the Prosecutor to do that, according to our criminal proceedings. Therefore, if the Defendant appearing in the criminal court of Yugoslavia says: "Yes, I did commit such and such an offence" and he explains why he committed that offence and under which circumstances, then he may be relieved of responsibility because of the absence of a criminal act if it is proven that he committed it in necessary self-defence, under extreme necessity, and duress is an element of extreme necessity. That is one point. Secondly, a Defendant, according to our law, may be relieved of criminal responsibility if it is proven that at the time of the commission of the act he was mentally irresponsible or that there was no direct or indirect premeditation. That is why my starting point was and remains that the statement of my Defendant is not ambiguous. By his statement, by his plea, he actually expressed his moral attitude towards the offence and the circumstances under which he committed that offence. Further, we are certainly not calling into question the statement of the accused, not even regarding his mental state, even though the first statement was made at a time when physicians said that he was suffering from Post Traumatic Stress Disorder, but he made such a statement before that, too, in the same mental state, after that, too, and under oath between this trial chamber as well, and especially that statement made under oath before the Chamber validates all the previous statements that he made. Therefore, we are not questioning it at all. PRESIDENT CASSESE: Thank you, Mr. Babic, but I do see that you still stick to the code -- the Yugoslav code of criminal procedure. I am afraid here in our Tribunal we do not apply any code of, say, Yugoslavia or France or Germany or, say, the United States of America. We apply our Statute, our Statute and our rules of procedure. Now under our Statute it is clear when you say "I plead guilty", that means that you regard yourself as criminally responsible, whereas if you say: "I plead guilty" and then immediately you say: "However, I murdered somebody but I say I acted in self-defence", that means in a way you negate your guilt and you do not regard yourself as guilty. You do not say "I am criminally responsible". You say "I did perpetrate an offence. I did act contrary to criminal law. However, I was excused by self-defence". In this case you cannot plead guilty. Anyway, I do not want to engage on a discussion on this point, but you should be aware again in our Statute, in our Tribunal, we have to apply the rules laid down in the Statute and the so-called Criminal Code, namely the rules of procedure and evidence. I wonder whether my colleagues have any question to put to Mr. Babic. Judge Li?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LI
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Counsel for the defence, I would like to ask you a question: could you cite a judgement rendered by a military Tribunal after World War 2 affirming a complete defence to a charge of killing innocent civilians under duress so that the accused was acquitted? My question is this. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BABIC
utterances.text: Your Honour Mr. Li, the judgements I had access to I referred to in my closing statement in the appeal and in the appellant's brief, these were mostly judgements rendered in 1947, 1948, when the main perpetrators for grave breaches of international humanitarian law were being tried. In all those judgements we see the position of the Nuremberg court that duress and superior orders cannot be accepted as exculpatory for the crimes committed by Fascist Germany and I stick to that to this day, but I do not find that those judgements are applicable to this case. In those judgements I never encountered duress as being accepted as excluding criminal responsibility, but I do not think that those cases are relative to this case, because we are talking about a regular enlisted man, a soldier. Those judgements do not refer to such lower rank military men. There is a well-known case in Yugoslavia, Soldier Schult, who was ordered with his unit to execute innocent people in Smedreska Palanta. He refused. There in front of those people who were later executed he was stripped of his rank, he was disarmed and later executed. There is a film in the archives of the Yugoslav cinematec, and it can be even seen, if necessary, as evidence material. Therefore, my reply is clearly in the judgments of 1947 and 1948 there were no such positions that you have referred to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LI
utterances.text: Thank you. You say that there is no judgment affirming -- there is no judgment rendered by a military Tribunal after World War 2 affirming a complete defence to a charge of killing innocent civilians under duress so that the accused was acquitted. You cannot find any judgement of military Tribunal to this effect. Is it so?

utterances.speaker: MR. BABIC
utterances.text: It is so, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LI
utterances.text: No precedent, no judicial precedent as to this question?

utterances.speaker: MR. BABIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct, but let me add again, I do not consider those judgements and those cases to be comparable with this case that is being tried here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LI
utterances.text: All right. Thank you very much. May I ask another question to the attorney for the prosecution? PRESIDENT CASSESE: If you do not mind, afterwards.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Mr. Babic, when Mr. Erdemovic entered his plea of duress, he pleaded guilty and asserted a plea of duress; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. BABIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: At that time was it his intention to assert it as a defence or as mitigation of punishment?

utterances.speaker: MR. BABIC
utterances.text: We are going back to the question, your Honour, of the purpose of the statement of the accused. That is a theoretical question. The statement of the accused has to be admitted both as evidence and as defence. Accepting one or the other would be inconsistent. If the accused Erdemovic in his testimony said that he was guilty because he participated or had to participate, as he put it, then that is both an accusation and a defence, but the prosecution did not provide any other evidence anyway, and we are not questioning that statement. The only evidence of that criminal offence is the statement by the accused. If that statement is admissible for such a grave crime, then it must be equally trustworthy regarding the conditions under which it was committed. So he did make that statement both as a plea of guilt and as a plea of defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Let us see if we can follow up a little bit on that. Was it your intention then when the plea of guilty was entered that if the trial Chamber accepted the plea of duress, that would result in no criminal punishment to the accused, or was it your intention that it be considered for the purpose of limiting the punishment that should be given to the accused?

utterances.speaker: MR. BABIC
utterances.text: My position and my argument of the plea is positioned alternatively. One is that all that I have said be admitted and the accused be acquitted, or if this reasoning of mine is not admitted and my defence is not admitted, taking into consideration all this that we are discussing, then that it should effect a significant mitigation of the sentence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: If I may just follow up on that, it appears from the sentencing judgement in paragraph 14 on page 7 the trial Chamber stated that: "The plea of duress may mitigate the penalty and, depending on the probative value and force which may be given to these factors, it might eliminate mens rea of the offence and therefore the offence itself". So at least it seems to me from my reading of this sentencing judgement that the trial Chamber was taking basically the same position that you have taken. Pardon me?

utterances.speaker: MR. BABIC
utterances.text: But it was not admitted in the final judgement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: I quite understand. They did not accept it. I accept that. It seems to me, although the judgement changes -- sometimes it refers to it as a defence; sometimes it is mitigating -- perhaps this must be the best for me at least explanation of what the Trial Chamber was intending, and that is that it may mitigate the penalty but depending on the probative value and force which may be given to it, that it might eliminate the mens rea of the offence and the offence itself. I understand your position that the Trial Chamber did not give it the value that you felt was appropriate. So, then, if I understand your position, you were asserting it both as a defence and as a mitigation; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. BABIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Now -- I am sorry. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. BABIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I am truly honoured to be the first attorney to appear at the appellate hearing of this Tribunal at which such extremely important issues are being discussed, and that is why I felt it was important that we reach some common understanding we should apply not only for this case but maybe for future cases as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: I have just another question, if I may. I gather that it is your position that the prosecution bears the burden of proving duress -- the absence of duress, because it is your position that it is a mens rea element or it is an element of the offence because of the mens rea requirement, and that the prosecution must then prove that the accused had this mens rea; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. BABIC
utterances.text: That is my position, and I think that is the position upheld by the criminal codes of European countries. The burden of proof is with the Prosecution, and it is not just the objective elements that have to be proven, but also the subjective elements or mens rea. So it is up to the Prosecution to prove that, which does not mean to say that the defence should take a passive attitude, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Mr. Akhavan, though, this morning stated with respect to duress mens rea and actus reus exist but duress as a defence I believe he said is only if there is no moral choice. Now, if you accept the proposition that even in a situation of duress mens rea exists, then would you still take the position that it is the burden of the Prosecution to prove the existence of mens rea in order to overcome a defence of duress, if you understand my question?

utterances.speaker: MR. BABIC
utterances.text: Yes, I quite understand. I said that the subjective elements of a criminal act are the question of competence, mental competence, and meditation. According to European codes you have to prove the objective elements, that somebody did commit an offence, the actual act, its consequences and the cause and effect -- those are the objective elements -- and the subjective elements, that somebody was mentally competent and his attitude towards that act, the mens rea, his mental attitude and his voluntary attitude, mentally whether he was conscious of what he was doing and, secondly, does he accept what he is doing? Does he have the will to do that? That is the law of European countries. That is the Prosecution -- up to the Prosecution to prove it. Of course the defence, too, if it is in its interest.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: But it may then prove mens rea and still the plea of duress may at the very least result in mitigation, and if that were the case, if the plea of duress is an issue of mitigation and not a defence, then would the defence have the burden of proving the validity of the plea of duress or would the Prosecution have the burden?

utterances.speaker: MR. BABIC
utterances.text: Let me refer again to the Criminal Code of Yugoslavia. According to the Yugoslav Criminal Code the court, irrespective of what the defence and the Prosecution asserts, can independently establish certain facts, regardless of what the parties submitted. In this case, whether duress has to be proven by the Prosecution or by the defence as a mitigating circumstance, we have tried to prove it, and I think we did prove it in the least as a mitigating circumstance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: One final question, Mr. President, if I may. The quote that you referred to, Mr. Babic, in your brief "to do evil to protect oneself against a crime is no evil", and you also referred in your opening comments this morning to self-defence, now that quote seems to me that that would raise an issue of self-defence, but that was not the plea that Mr. Erdemovic entered when he entered his plea of guilty. He was not claiming self-defence, was he?

utterances.speaker: MR. BABIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, you have made a very good point, but it is true that this quotation is reminiscent of self-defence, but it is also reminiscent of extreme necessity as a second institution. Necessary self-defence excludes the existence of an offence and there is another one, that is extreme necessity, too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Thank you. PRESIDENT CASSESE: Thank you. I would like to ask one further question.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone please, your Honour. PRESIDENT CASSESE: I am sorry. I am not very good with this equipment. It is too complicated for me. If you do not mind, Mr. Babic, I would like to ask you a second question, which does not relate to the issue of guilty plea -- or I mean not to the extent -- it is a bit different from the various problems we have been discussing so far. You know that Mr. Erdemovic was charged by the Prosecutor on the same facts for war crimes or crimes against humanity. Now when he entered a guilty plea, he pleaded guilty to crimes against humanity. My question is as follows: did you explain to him the difference between war crimes and crimes against humanity? In particular, did you explain to Mr. Erdemovic that, all things being equal, to classify an offence as crime against humanity normally entails a heavier penalty than that consequent upon a war crime? For instance, if somebody is charged with murdering, say, ten persons or five persons, now if this murder which occurs during an armed conflict is classified as a war crime, normally it entails a less heavy penalty than the same murder if it is classified as a crime against humanity because of the stigma which attaches to crimes against humanity and also because, as the Trial Chamber pointed out in its decision, a crime against humanity is a crime committed not only against somebody, the persons who are killed, but also against humanity as a whole. The victim is not only the person who is actually killed but also the whole of mankind. So did you clarify to your client the difference between these two classes of crimes, because I have seen -- we have all seen that actually he pleaded guilty to the more serious crime. This is my question to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BABIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, before the accused Erdemovic entered his plea as to what he felt he was guilty of, he was questioned by the esteemed colleague from the Prosecution. When all this came together and when he entered his plea and when this was compared with the legal solution set forth in the Statute as to what is the essence of the criminal offence of the war crime and what is the essence of the criminal offence of the crime against humanity, taking into account the absence of war operations, combat operations and bearing in mind the presence of the civilian population, there was no other choice. We did not have the option of war crime, because the elements -- all the elements of the criminal offence of the war crime were not present. So we discussed that. PRESIDENT CASSESE: Sorry. May I ask you -- I did not understand you correctly. You said that some elements of war crimes were not present. Which elements of war crimes were not present?

utterances.speaker: MR. BABIC
utterances.text: Yes. PRESIDENT CASSESE: Which ones?

utterances.speaker: MR. BABIC
utterances.text: The presence of the civilian population is not an element of the war crime; it is an element of the crime against humanity. PRESIDENT CASSESE: Do you mean to say that in an armed conflict, whatever its classification, whether it is classified as internal or international, the killing of civilians may not be regarded as a war crime? I mean, if you go through the case law of --

utterances.speaker: MR. BABIC
utterances.text: During combat operations, yes, during combat operations. PRESIDENT CASSESE: All right. Thank you. Now I think we can now move on to the Prosecutor, and I think we have quite a few questions -- I for one have quite a few questions to ask the Prosecutor. I wonder whether my colleagues would mind if I ask and I will probably give up some of my questions. Probably there are too many. First of all, there is an issue which has just been discussed between Judge McDonald and the defence counsel, namely what actually defence counsel did when he raised the question of duress, whether he urged duress as a defence or as a mitigating circumstance. Now, the Prosecutor in his written brief states, and I quote: "The guilty plea entered by the accused was unequivocal in that the accused invoked duress only in mitigation of his sentence and not as a defence". Now, this is in conflict -- this is contrary both with what -- contrary both to what the defence counsel has just pointed out and also to what actually happened in the various stages of the proceedings before the Trial Chamber. Let me also quote a few passages of those transcripts. This was on 31st May, I think. When Mr. Erdemovic entered the guilty plea, he said and I quote -- it is page 9 of that transcript, Friday, 31st May 1996, page 9, lines 7-11. He said and I quote: "Your Honour, I had to do this", namely to kill the civilians. "If I had refused, I would have been killed together with the victims. When I refused they told me: "If you are sorry for them, stand up, line up with them and we will kill you too. I'm not sorry for myself, but for my family, my wife and son, who I then had nine months but I could not refuse because then they would have killed me. That is all I wish to add". At that stage it was not clarified whether this statement was made to urge mitigation of the sentence or whether it was urged as a defence proper. So, as I say, this point was not clarified. However, later on in the closing statement, closing argument of the defence lawyer, which I quoted before, clearly, as he just pointed out, the question of duress or necessity was again urged both as a defence proper, and therefore quite consistently he insisted that Mr. Erdemovic be acquitted, as well as a mitigating circumstance, and he requested that a very lenient sentence be passed. So, therefore, I do not understand why you make this statement which I just mentioned before, and I would like to ask you whether you could clarify this point?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Certainly, your Honour. Your Honours, the position of the Prosecution on this is that the issue of the guilty plea was explained in great detail by the sentencing court, and even when this question arose, it was explained again. In addition to that there is the rules of the Tribunal, which speak of a sentencing hearing in Rule 92, I think -- sorry -- Rule 62, paragraph 5. Once the plea of guilty is entered, then a date for the pre-sentencing hearing takes place. So there is in the rules itself -- it is implicit, in our submission, that one moves immediately from the plea to the sentencing issue. That was understood, we submit, by the accused and his counsel. The sentencing judge himself at page 6 of the transcript of 31st May 1996 at line 22, we submit, starts off by setting out what is understood by a plea of guilty, and he clearly says: "If you plead not guilty, you will be entitled to a trial during which, of course, with your lawyer, you will contest the charges and allegations and the charges presented against you by the Prosecutor. As I will remind you, alternatively, either one of the other violation was of the crimes against humanity or war crimes..." His Honour goes on. Then at line 26 he says: "If you plead not guilty the trial will continue but completely differently, which I am sure you understand, but which I have to explain to you. At that point you will have the opportunity during another hearing and a date which we will set at that point in agreement with everybody you will plead guilty but you will plead under other circumstances, that is that there are attenuating circumstances, mitigating circumstances or aggravating circumstances. Then there will be a discussion between your attorney and the Prosecution, which will not be the same". Now that was explained, in our submission, right at the outset. Then at the point your Honour, the learned President, took us to, you say that he raises here an equivocal plea. We submit not. What he raises here is, and what we say is instructive about this is line 9, where he says: "I am not sorry for myself but for my family, my wife and son we then had nine months and I could not refuse because then they would have killed me". In our submission, your Honour, this is raised at this point. His Honour the presiding judge then moves immediately on to the question. He says at line 14: "Mr. Erdemovic, would you please rise again? The Tribunal must be sure that you know what you are doing, because you know that pleading guilty or not guilty does not have the same consequences. You are before a Tribunal and the Tribunal must determine a penalty for your behaviour. At the proper time it will do so, and, of course, at the end of this one how we are going to organise the second one where you can explain yourself, but you cannot go back on the facts to which you have pleaded guilty. This is finished now and this is something that the Tribunal wants to be sure you really understand, and that your plea is sincere. You are represented by Mr. Babic. Are you satisfied with his representation, with your counsel? Have you been able to discuss things with your attorney under the most desirable conditions?" The accused responds: "Your Honour, I am satisfied with the indictment". His Honour then says, and I labour this point because it I will states the very point. His Honour then insists: "This is not the indictment now I am talking about. I want to know whether through the contacts that you have had were you able to have counsel of your choice? If I ask you this question it is because the Tribunal had to appoint counsel". His Honour goes on to speak about the appointment of counsel. Then at the bottom of the page, line 32, page 9: "Therefore, from this point on, you have given up the right to a trial to determine whether or not you are guilty. This must be clear. This must be clear to you, clear between you and the Tribunal ...", and so on. I do not need to labour it any further. The point I make, your Honour, is at that stage his honour the presiding judge of the sentencing Chamber was meticulous to ensure that the accused and his counsel knew what was happening. There is a confusion, your Honours, and the confusion is simply this, and I think Mr. Babic points to it in his appeal papers when he says there is a collision between two jurisdictions. We submit there is no collision, because the international law position is very clear and duress is simply not available or open to the accused, but what the collision is, your Honour, is the fact that notwithstanding what the sentencing judge was saying, notwithstanding what was in the rules about what was happening and the great lengths that His Honour the Presiding Judge went to try and ensure that the accused knew what he was doing, the accused through his counsel continually went back to the position where he wanted it to be both ways. This was notwithstanding the fact that the judge explained it. So there is either two things here. One is he could not understand or did not understand what the judge was saying to him, or alternatively he refused to understand. Our submission is at the time he entered his plea of guilty he knew what he was doing. He was saying: "Yes, I committed this crime, but I want to say to you that I did so because I had to protect my wife and child", who he was concerned about. "I was not concerned about myself. It was not a circumstance where I genuinely feared that there would be immediate reaction to me disobeying this order". I pointed out the fact, your Honours, on two other occasions he had disobeyed orders. He was not concerned then that there would be immediate reaction. He was concerned about his wife and child, so he says. He said that: "I want your Honours to take that into account when you are sentencing me". That was clear. That was very clear. Just touching on the issue of whether that position changed, in so far as the accused is concerned, it never changed. In our submission, the accused himself maintained the same position throughout. PRESIDENT CASSESE: Mr. Prosecutor, on one small point still I do not understand you when you say he was only concerned about his wife and child, because as I said before, I quoted Mr. Erdemovic's statement here when he pleaded guilty. He said: "When I refused to shoot, they told me: "If you are sorry for them, stand up, line up with them, and we will kill you too". Then he goes on to say: "I was also sorry for my family, my wife and my son". So, therefore, he was also concerned about his own life. Anyway, I agree with you in a way it was clear throughout the proceedings that the counsel for defence did not perceive the real import and scope and significance of guilty plea notion under our Statute. However, it is a fact that he insisted all over again on both his client being guilty and on necessity, on necessity. So I wonder whether this by itself would not make the guilty plea ambiguous, but let me move on to a different point, if you allow me. Now this morning Mr. Akhavan has stated again what was forcefully pointed out in your written submission, and I quote Mr. Akhavan, namely there is overwhelming evidence to the effect that duress cannot be urged as a defence in case of murder. I wonder whether this is correct, because actually in your written statement you mention three cases, two British cases and one Canadian case, but quite properly you also say that there is another British case, Wepson case, and two US cases before the Nuremberg Military Tribunal -- the American Military Tribunal sitting at Nuremberg which took a different position. Therefore it is not true that there is an overwhelming weight of evidence, but on top of that I would like to add that I am sure you are aware that there are quite a few other cases which take a different position, namely a position whereby duress may be pleaded as a defence even in case of murder or in any cases where important tribunals do not make any distinction between the underlying crime. Let me just quote the Eichmann case, the Supreme Court of Israel; two French cases, Touvier, T-O-U-V-I-E-R, judgements by a Court of Appeal and Court of Cassation in France, and P-A-P-O-N, the Papon case; as well as a recent Italian case, P-R-I-E-B-K-E, Priebke. Let me just read out and ask you to comment on one small passage from the Israeli case. This is from the international law reports volume 36 and it is the judgement delivered by the Supreme Court of Israel. There they say and I quote: "As stated, the applicability of these defences, namely constraint or necessity, as relieving from responsibility in respect of the offences the subject of the law of 1950" -- this is an Israeli law of 1950 -- "has been excluded by Section 11 there". I think it is a very bad translation. The point comes now. They go on to say, and I quote: "But even had the Israeli law permitted the accused to rely on the defence that in carrying out the order to commit the crime he was acting in circumstances of constraint or necessity, he would still not succeed unless the following two facts were proved: one, that danger to his life was imminent; two, that he carried out the criminal task out of a desire to save his own life and because he knew of no other possibility of doing so". Then they quote the Einsatzgruppen case. Then they go on to say: "As will be seen below, neither of the said conditions has been met in this case". Then I have again for your comments an Italian case where, as in the case of Eichmann -- as you know, Eichmann was accused of planning the genocide of millions of Jews. Now this is a case which came up before the Italian Military Court in Rome. The accused, Captain Priebke, he was a Captain of the SS, he was accused of complicity in the killing of quite a few people. Again it is a murder case. There the Tribunal pointed out the following, and I will read slowly the relevant passage: "The Tribunal observes that had the accused faced an imminent threat of death, he would no longer have been under a duty to refuse the order, as he would have been acting in a state of necessity". Then it went on to say: "In this event of imminent threat of death he have could have backed down from refusing to obey an order and participated in the executions only to save his own life, claiming the defence of state of necessity, which is provided for in all legal orders, including German law. Indeed, in this case, no person could have expected Priebke", the German captain, "to act as a hero and sacrifice his own life in order to avoid participating in the inhumane execution, the execution of 335 civilians. Thus, in all of the possibilities with which we have dealt Priebke could have had a way out. This way out, however, certainly could not be that of obeying a manifestly unlawful order except in case of imminent danger to his life. As such danger was never realistically made apparent in this case, it follows that he has full responsibility as an accomplice with other executioners". Therefore, the court rejected the defence of duress on point of fact. I wonder if you could comment on these cases and in a way elaborate on the philosophy of your view of duress as only a mitigating circumstance in case the underlying crime is a murder.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I will ask Mr. Akhavan to give me some assistance in this, because he has done a particular study of the international cases and other cases relating to this. I would like to comment generally, if I may, on the matters that were raised by your Honours. It has never been the position of the Prosecution that there is not a division of opinion among the various national states with respect to the question of whether or not duress can be a defence, especially when the underlying offence involves a killing of innocent human beings. Our argument is, and I will ask Mr. Akhavan to develop this for your Honour, is that in international law, and the law we would urge your Honours to apply, we would say that applying that law, your Honours, duress is not a defence to a crime where the underlying offence involves the killing of innocent human beings. We say that although there is perhaps strong and compelling arguments in favour of why some jurisdictions would admit duress as a defence, we say there is equally some strong and compelling reasons why it should not be admitted as an offence, especially when it involves the killing of innocent human beings. We say that it is appropriate for your Honours to apply the international law, and in that respect we would reinforce that by referring to the strong underlying principles which would suggest that it should not be a defence. If I may, and if it would assist your Honours, the case that I referred to by Lord Salmon is very instructive on this point. If I may, I will read out the passage because I think it may assist in an understanding of at least the policy considerations as to why it should not be admitted as a defence. His Honour -- his Lordship Lord Salmon first deals with the case of Lynch v the Director of Public Prosecutions, which had admitted duress to attempted murder. Then he makes a comment that -- he says: "There is no case in England or any other part of the Commonwealth" bearing in mind this was Privy Council "that duress is an defence to a charge of murder by a principal in the first degree". He points to one exception in South Africa and says that is a combination of Roman, Dutch and English law. Then he says this: "Counsel for the appellant has argued that the law presupposes a degrees of heroism, of which the ordinary man is incapable and which therefore should not be expected of him and modern conditions and concepts of humanity have rendered obsolete the rule that the actual killer cannot rely on duress as a defence. Their Lordships do not agree. In the trial of those responsible for war crime atrocities such as mass killings of men, women and children, inhuman experiments on human beings often resulting in death and like crimes it was invariably argued for the defence that these atrocities should be excused on the grounds they resulted from superior records and duress. If the accused had refused to do these dreadful things they would have been shot and therefore they should be acquitted and allowed to go free. This argument has always been universally rejected. Their Lordships would be sorry indeed to see it accepted by the common law of England. It seems incredible to their Lordships that in any civilised society any such acts as the appellant's, whatever threats may have been made to him, could be regarded as excusable or within the law. We are not living in a dream world in which the mounting wave of violence and terrorism can be contained by strict logic and intellectual niceties alone. Common sense surely reveals the added dangers to which in these modern times in the modern world the public would be exposed if the change in the law proposed on behalf of the appellants was effected. It might as well, as Lord Simon of Glysdale said in Lynch's case, prove to be a charter for terrorists, gang leaders and kidnappers". His Honour then goes on to hypothesise what would happen if this defence was permitted, and how terrorists might put under duress other parties who could go and plant a bomb in a market place, on a plane or elsewhere. People would be killed en masse, and then it may be used again by terrorists to do the very same thing. We submit that these policy considerations, coupled with the international law itself, is in our submission why duress should not be permitted. To answer your Lordship's question relating to the international law, I will ask my friend to address you. PRESIDENT CASSESE: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. AKHAVAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would like to point out first, of course that in terms of the respective authority of the cases which you have mentioned that all of these are cases before domestic courts, and they are, I believe, applying domestic law or perhaps the domestic interpretation of the applicable international law. With respect to these cases, one clearly sees in terms of the higher archive of sources for international law under Article 38, paragraph 1 of the Statute of the International Court Of Justice, that judicial decisions are only subsidiary sources of international law. They are clearly not the primary or decisive source for determination of norms. Of course, when a court is in its decision reflecting international law, whether it is conventional, customary or otherwise, then it can be given more weight. I would submit that the decisions in the Touvier, Papon and Priebke cases in no way contradict the earlier submission I made today and the submission we have may have had in writing in the sense that these are all civil law jurisdictions in which clearly duress has a broad applications, which includes the crime of murder. The Eichmann case may be somewhat different, but the Eichmann case is also referring back to the erroneous judgement of the Einsatzgruppen trial. First of all, I would have to inspect more closely the specific facts that are involved when the court made the statement which your Honour referred to, but my understanding once again from what you have read is that the court is referring back to the Einsatzgruppen trial. The reason why I am saying that the overwhelming authority is against the proposition is based on the few assumptions. The first assumption is that the report of the United Nations War Crimes Commission, which I have reproduced for your Honours -- I may be able to hand the relevant parts -- in Volume 15, which deals with the plea of duress, has isolated the leading cases or actually the only cases which are on point with respect to duress. I believe that those cases must be given considerably more weight than any national decision in the sense that all of those cases were applying international law, even though some of them were national courts of the occupying powers. The control council power number 10 was adopted by the four allied powers and 19 additional signatories, such that one can consider it as part of the corpus of international law. From those decisions you have pointed out a number of cases which go contrary to our position. The Wepson I case was decided before a British military Tribunal. It was decided in 1946, and was effectively overruled by the two subsequent decisions of the British cases in the Stalag Luft III case and in the Furstein case, which were decided in 1947 and 1948 respectively. Also in 1946 a Canadian Military Tribunal in the Holzer case had decided the contrary position. The Wepson trial cites no authority whatsoever in support of its proposition, contrary to the three other decisions which we have spoken of. Certainly when a court does not cite any authority in support of its proposition, its statement cannot be given the same weight as that of the three other courts. In the US cases as well, as we have pointed out, the IG Farben, Krupp and Flick cases are not on point. They do not deal with the question of killing. At most there is a passing reference to this question in Krupp based on an obscure commentary from 1932. It is our submission that that cannot be given any significant weight. Similarly the Einsatzgruppen trial does not produce any authority in support of its proposition. As we have pointed out, even had they wanted to, they would not have found anything in international law. They would not have found any precedent as of that point in time which would support their proposition, nor even in their own American law would they have found any support for that proposition. So I do not think that one can say that the reference to the erroneous judgement of the Einsatzgruppen trial, the erroneous reference in subsequent decisions such as Eichmann in any way invalidates the argument which we have made. If I may also clarify one small point, your Honours, that refers back to the question of mens rea, the question of duress as an excuse. What I was trying to explain, your Honours, is simply that there is no reason why duress categorically must apply to the crime of murder. Unlike justification, it is not a defence which in all respects removes the criminal character of the crime in question. I refer here to the 1996 report of the International Law Commission in its commentary on the Draft Code of Crimes against the Peace and Security of Mankind at page 74. The Commission recognises the distinction between justifications and excuses and goes on to say as follows: "Self-defence is a justification eliminating in all respects the criminal character in question", but the Commission goes on to recognise specifically that: "Duress, if admitted in relation to particular crime, is merely an excuse which may exculpate a particular accused". What we are simply trying to point out, your Honour, is that the question of where one draws the line as to the application of this defence is one which is determined variously in differing legal systems. In order to decide where to draw that line in international law, one has to refer back to the leading authorities, which we submit are those cited by the UN War Crimes Commission, and on the weight all support the proposition that duress should never apply as a defence to murder. If you have no further questions ... PRESIDENT CASSESE: Thank you. I think it is time --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: I would just like to take up with you the question of the distinction that is apparently drawn in the report to which you have just referred between self-defence and duress. How do you understand the basis for that distinction? In each case the act is done consciously and voluntarily, "voluntarily" in quotes, if you like, because of an overwhelming need either to defend yourself or to save yourself from threatened duress. What is the distinction between the two?

utterances.speaker: MR. AKHAVAN
utterances.text: If I may quote on that point, your Honour, the comments of Smith and Hogan once again on the English law, whereby they say: "An act is justified when we positively approve of that". When someone kills in self-defence or even one can give the example of someone administering a death penalty, one is not engaging --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: But the administration of a death penalty is entirely different. That is a state servant carrying out the order of a court. Let us get back to self-defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. AKHAVAN
utterances.text: In both cases, as Smith and Hogan would explain, the behaviour is approved of. The act in question is approved of, whereas when an act is merely excused, it is disapproved of, but we think not to treat it as a crime. So in the case of self-defence, the act in question, the actual killing, which is committed in self-defence, is approved of, and one can also say that the mens rea the element of the guilty mind, does not exist, whereas in the case of an excuse the act itself is disapproved of. It involves a guilty mind, but there is exculpation for reasons -- what I would consider to be reasons of public policy cited from the case from the Supreme Court of Canada based on societal expectations of what is reasonable pressure, what is reasonable resistance to pressure. But the point is simply that it is very clear from the different legal systems of the world that self-defence is seen as a categorical defence. It is always a defence when the requisite elements are present, but duress is not so. Duress is applied in very different ways, not only between the civil law and Common Law systems, but within the Common Law systems themselves based on various considerations of public policy, of societal expectations as to what may legitimately be expected of the reasonable person when subjected to certain pressure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: All I want -- I do not want a question. The case that you referred to, you did not refer to in your brief. Could you provide a copy of that case?

utterances.speaker: MR. AKHAVAN
utterances.text: Certainly, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: If you could provide it so that I can look at it over the recess, it would help me.

utterances.speaker: MR. AKHAVAN
utterances.text: I will do it immediately. PRESIDENT CASSESE: Before we break for 20 minutes may I just point out, however, that you insist on the authorities given by some cases -- in some cases, the Stalag Luft III case, the Furstein and the Holzer case, but these authorities are British authorities. I know very well. They keep quoting Dudley and Stephen. So again they are within the national approach. You cannot make a difference between other courts which apply national law, as you said, and then these three cases which you very much emphasise because they are blind to national law. No, not at all. To the best of my recollection they simply quote British cases, in particular the famous Minionette case. So again I do not see any difference between these various classes of cases. Again I do not see why 3 out of 20 cases should remain and be regarded as the overwhelming weight of evidence in international law, but this is a point we can take up later on. I think it is high time for a break. I suggest to adjourn for 20 minutes. The meeting stands adjourned. (11.20 am) (Short break) (11.40 am) PRESIDENT CASSESE: Before we start with questions for the Prosecutor, may I tell you that we have decided to go on until 1 o'clock and then to adjourn and resume at 2.30. Is that agreeable to you? Thank you. Now let us go on with questions to the Prosecutor. I have one final question, which relates to, as Mr. Niemann put it, policy considerations of policy issues behind the question of duress and also the basic issue of whether or not there really exists a split, it is a different approach between civil law and Common Law countries. Let me try to clarify with you this issue by in a way submitting to you four different cases or instances and by discussing these four different instances we may see whether actually there exists a difference between, as I say, civil law countries and Common Law countries, and also we could probably try to pinpoint the philosophy behind the notion of duress and why in Common Law countries duress may not be urged as defence in case of murder. One first case is very simple. A person, A, compels at gunpoint a person, B, to kill a third, C. A, B, C. A tells B if he cannot kill C, he himself will be shot dead. It is very clear the person must choose between his life and the life of a third person. This is the most elementary case. This is the case normally dealt with by quite a few judgements, including those which you have mentioned. There are also some judgements delivered by the French military courts after the Second World War, where we have precisely this situation, a captain telling a soldier: "If you do not kill that civilian, I will kill you". Therefore the person coerced, as I say, has to choose between his own life and the life of a third person. Then we have the slightly more complicated case. The person A tells B if he does not kill C he will kill the child of B. Here the person coerced must choose between the life of a third person and the life of his own child, but still probably we still remain within the approach, within the framework of the choice between the life of an innocent person and the life of that person who is requested to shoot. Then I think we may move on to a different situation. Let me give you two examples there, two instances which I have thought up. One may be regarded as typical of, say, our own countries' situation in time of peace. Say a bank robbery case. A person, say a robber, after taking hostage another person, requests a witness of the hostage taking to kill the hostage. The robber, say A, adds that if C, namely the witness, does not execute the hostage he will shoot both the hostage and the witness. Now in this case the person coerced must choose between shooting the hostage or being killed together with the hostage. So the witness, therefore, knows that in any case the hostage will be killed. Could one then say that by killing the hostage he chooses the lesser of two evils? As I say, he knows that in any case the hostage will be killed. So his choice is very limited. "Either we both die or he will die, and he will die in any case. He will be shot either by me or by the hostage taker". Then a similar example that is more germane to a warlike situation, and I will say the example is as follows. The member of an execution squad upon his refusal to take part in the execution of ten prisoners of war is threatened to be shot right away. No other member of that execution squad refuses to obey the order to kill the POWs. In this case the person under duress must decide whether to sacrifice his own life knowing, and this is my major point, knowing that the ten prisoners of war will be shot anyway. He is not faced with a real choice between his own life and that of other persons. Now do you see the difference, because in a way if you think of the first two cases I very much doubt in a civil law country judges would take a position different from that of a Common Law court. Probably even of a civil law country the philosophy which you mentioned before and which you in a way propounded so well, the philosophy you set out, the philosophy behind duress not being a defence in case of murder. Probably that philosophy would also apply in a civil law country. Why? Because again there is the choice between my life and the life of an innocent person. Of course, this in particular applies when I am a soldier. I am a combatant, and therefore because of my own profession, I have to face risks, whereas the innocent person is not a combatant. He is just a civilian. So, therefore, as I say, even in a civil law country we, -- I think a court would stick to your philosophy. Probably with some doubts between a choice of being killed or the child being killed, my second example. I have to choose between killing a third person or killing -- seeing my child killed by the person who is coercing me, but if you think of the third or fourth case, there in any case you know there is no choice, because in any case, as I said, either the witness and the hostage both will be killed or ten prisoners of war will be killed. Could you comment on these various cases and see whether you could apply your philosophy? To what extent what you find as the rationale behind the three cases you are insisting upon, whether this rationale can also apply to all the four cases or only to some of them?

utterances.speaker: MR. AKHAVAN
utterances.text: Well, your Honour, this is, of course, an exceedingly complex philosophical discussion. One could discuss this from very different perspectives. If the underlying issue is the proportionality of evil, as you are suggesting, then one would have to measure what is the evil in each particular situation, which is avoided as opposed to the evil which is committed, but that is not as easy an exercise as it may appear to be. Even if one reduces it to a pure game of numbers, which I think is problematic from several points of view, to say it is better to take one life than allow two to be killed, even if one accepts that premise, there are still wider considerations of public policy.
