Is such a defence going to be open to abuse? Is it going to open a Pandora's box? Is it going to creates ambiguities in a certain area of criminal law where there should be none? Is the evil which is avoided by saving two lives rather than killing one, does it not also take into account the evil in that occasion of allowing such a defence? I think what I was trying to explain in the beginning is that this is essentially a very imprecise moral and philosophical discussion we are engaging in. It is very clear different societies deal with it differently. In France the notion of "contrainte" applies to all crimes, even murder. In Canada not only does it not apply to murder; it also does not apply to causing grave bodily harm, it does not apply to sexual assault, it does not apply to kidnapping. Essentially what we are dealing with are different societal expectations which is the reason I quoted that Supreme Court of Canada case just as an example of how different systems recognise that there is no categorical imperative, there is no absolute reason for applying duress to all crimes. For reasons of public policy, for considerations of what society will accept as reasonable resistance to pressure certain crimes may be exempt. If any injustice is to be done to the Defendant, that can be dealt with by way of mitigation. It can be dealt with, for example, through the remission of a sentence. The problem, your Honour, is if we are going to resolve this issue based on this abstract philosophical discussion, it will be extremely problematical from the point of view even of the nullem crimen principle. To the extent possible we should reduce this discussion to a rather positive discussion, if I may say, of what is the applicable law under international law? That is the reason why, in our submission, we have pointed to what we believe are the most authoritative cases in international law. I wish to explain that when considering decisions such as Priebke, Papon, Touvier or the Eichmann trial, as distinct from the decisions of the post-World War II tribunals, one has to make an analysis of the authority to be attributed to these sources. We are dealing with a system in which there is considerable ambiguity because of the absence of a Sovereign legislature. One has to make a careful enquiry as to what weight is to be given to these various sources. We would submit clearly that the Nuremberg judgement and Charter is beyond doubt part of the customary international law, as recognised in the report of the Secretary General. We would further submit that the Control Council Law Number 10, which was adopted by fifteen states upon conclusion of the Second World War is also beyond doubt part of customary international lawful. This is also recognised by the report of the Secretary General, by the Resolution 95 of the General Assembly in 1946, and so on and so forth. That core area is a core area of certainty. The domestic cases of various jurisdictions can only create confusion. Now, one way of considering this discussion is to turn it around and to say: could we say that duress is applicable to murder as a defence? If one was to go with that position, then one would ignore not only the relevant international authority, but even if one bases it entirely on domestic legal systems, then one would have to ignore the position of a significant number of domestic systems. PRESIDENT CASSESE: Sorry to interrupt you, but I think you are missing my point. Probably I did not make myself clear. First of all, you have to choose between positive law -- you are mentioning positive law on the one side and then reasons of public policy on the other side. You have to choose. I mean, you cannot move from one point of view to another. These are two different approaches.

utterances.speaker: MR. AKHAVAN
utterances.text: If I may clarify, your Honour -- PRESIDENT CASSESE: You are saying public international law is clear on this matter because of three judgements you are quoting and then at least 25 judgements can be quoted to the contrary. Therefore, probably public international law is not very clear on this matter. What I want to now explore with you is the rationale behind those three judgements, namely the British cases, the famous Dudley and Stephen and even Howe, which we know very well, and try to understand whether this rationale can apply in those other cases and actually even be applied, say, in civil law courts as well as in international tribunals. Now, as I say, the rationale of this court is you cannot choose between your own life and the life of an innocent person. These are the so-called reasons of public policy which you very well emphasised in your statement and the statement of Mr. Niemann. However, my point was totally different. I said that you have two different situations, a situation where you have this choice and then you make the wrong choice, if you wish, because you then kill somebody else for the sake of not sacrificing your own life. Then you have a different situation where you have no choice at all, because you know that you are a member of a ten member execution squad. You see that the other nine, all of them are prepared to shoot the ten prisoners of war, and you are faced with this option, because your captain said: "Look, if you do not also take part in the killing, I will shoot you". Now in this case, as I say, by sacrificing your life you do not save the life of the ten people, prisoners of war, because in any case they are going to be shot. Is there a real moral choice in this case? Do you not see the difference between the other case where you have to choose between your life and the life of somebody else? In the very elementary case where you have three people, one tells the other one: "If you do not shoot the third person, I will shoot you". There you have to choose and then a soldier -- I agree with the rationale behind the British case law. I agree that a soldier should not sacrifice the life of an innocent person, and because of his profession, because of moral duties, because of his habit to kill and his profession to be somebody who shoots and kills combatants, he has to sacrifice his own life. This is the philosophy between Dudley and Stephen and Howe. You see the case is totally different in the case I have offered you for your comments. I would like you to comment on the case of the ten POWs and the member of the execution squad and tell me has he got any real choice, knowing that in any case the POWs will be killed? Is there any point in his sacrificing his own life? Should he be requested to be a hero so for historic record in the future people will say: "He refuse to take part in a killing", but for what purpose?

utterances.speaker: MR. AKHAVAN
utterances.text: First of all, I would be very interested to know once again what the international authority is on this particular scenario which you have posed, but even so the question once again of making a distinction between various concepts, for one thing, yes, I would argue that even in such a scenario where the killing of one life may save ten that there may be sound reasons in law not to permit a complete defence but to compensate for the lack of moral choice through other means such as sentencing. I think this is exactly the thinking behind the Common Law position. What I tried to say when I was distinguishing between an excuse and a justification is that there is no categorical reason for saying that duress must necessarily apply. It may or may not based on one's expectations of what is reasonable under the circumstances, based on one's expectations of the harm which creation of such a defence may create for such a society at large. Now we are not -- perhaps I should clarify. We are not necessarily making an argument of public policy here. We are trying to reduce the equation to the point possible, to a series of decisions which we believe have to be the core of the law which is applied by this court. Now if I may elaborate briefly once again on those cases, firstly, it is clear that one could -- at some point there has to be a delimitation of the sources of law which we are going to use in order to make a determination on this question. Many of the courts which have dealt with this question in civil law countries have simply applied the civil law. The French decisions which you have cited I am not aware of, but the French cases which were decided pursuant to Control Council law number 10, I am not aware of any case which specifically states that duress may be admitted as a defence to murder. Even if that were the case, surely the French courts would have relied on their own system, as the British courts relied on theirs. The question is: are we going to reduce this to a question of a contest between the Common Law and the civil law? I would submit that the court should not make this a contest between two systems, because it does not have to. As I was trying to explain, the fact that the British courts relied on the laws of their own country may or may not be problematic, but through the past fifty years that body of law has become beyond doubt part of customary law. We cannot now go back fifty years and question the sources which they have relied on. Frankly speaking, the courts had no other sources to rely on. There was nothing in international law which they could have relied on. There was nothing under the general principles of law which they could rely on. One could even say that the court made an arbitrary decision. The British court, realising that it cannot rely on any clear precedent, simply said: "We will apply the law of the House of Lords". That law has not been contested or disputed and it is now part of customary law, just as conspiracy, a concept wholly alien to the civil law system, is. I am sure the contrary is true. One could cite a number of Roman law maxims which have been introduced into international law. One could not now say because they pertain to the Roman legal system that they should not be admissible. I would go further and say we are presupposing there is only the Common Law and civil law. There are many other legal systems. One could go on really an endless expedition of analysing what different legal systems have to say. Going, if I may, just quickly back to the case law, our submission is that only the Einsatzgruppen trial from the law which this court should apply goes contrary to our position. Even the High Command case, which is often cited as authority, does not deal with this specific issue. In the High Command case the statement in passing on duress is made in a section entitled "superior orders" and the defence in that case was suggesting, if I may just quote quickly: "To recognise as a defence to the crimes set forth in Control Council law number 10 that a Defendant acted pursuant to the order of his government or of a superior would be in practical effect to say that all the guilt charged in the indictment was the guilt of Hitler alone, because he alone possessed the law-making power of the State and the Supreme authority to issue civil and military directives". This is at page 12 of my oral submission: "To recognise such a contention would be to recognise an absurdity". Now that is what the court was dealing with. It was that defence of superior orders and not duress. So even the High Command case is really not on point. At best its ambiguous formulation may be considered as obiter dicta. Even in the Einsatzgruppen trial the court never seriously considered the defence of duress. The case, of course, dealt with the extermination squads of Einsatzgruppen in Eastern Europe, which had slaughtered thousands and thousands of people. I do not think the court at any point gave any serious consideration to the proposition that people who had engaged in an orgy of slaughter over several years could seriously raise the defence of duress. What I mean to say, your Honour, is that the court in the Einsatzgruppen case did not really make a serious enquiry as to what the applicable law is. The fact that what I consider to be an erroneous decision is now repeated in subsequent commentaries, in the Eichmann case, for example, does not give it any more legitimacy than it had to begin with. I would also add once again that the leading commentators on international law have not simply objected to this case but, to quote Sir Hersch Lauterpacht, have expressed serious objections to the reasoning of the court. Yoram Dinstein, an Israeli international lawyer, goes as far as to say it is most unfortunate that the court has decided this is a defence of unlimited application, because hypothetically if it is a defence of unlimited application, it could justify a number of scenarios which for various reasons would not be in the best interests of international law as a system. So I hope that clarifies our position, your Honour. PRESIDENT CASSESE: Thank you very much indeed. Before I ask my colleagues whether they have questions to ask you, let me say that I very much admire the calm way you have responded to my questions and I apologise nor being a bit passionate and vehement. I did not intend to be aggressive, not at all. I am just so excited by these important questions. I think these are crucial issues. Again I apologise. I would like to ask my colleagues whether they have any questions: Judge McDonald?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: I have a few, and I will try to be as passionate as President Cassese. I can be. I want to return for a moment to this motion of whether or not the plea was equivocal, and I want to discuss self-defence as opposed to duress. Now, if the accused had pleaded self-defence that, of course, would have been an equivocal plea, because there is no mens rea to commit murder, as you have said. There is no mens rea because the notion of self-defence is that you are protecting yourself against the perpetrator and that at least in my system you may use only such force as is necessary to protect yourself. So there would be no mens rea in that situation and thus there would be an equivocal plea; is that so?

utterances.speaker: MR. AKHAVAN
utterances.text: Yes. I would submit that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Because it is a justification. You cannot plead guilty if what you are pleading to is a justification.

utterances.speaker: MR. AKHAVAN
utterances.text: Clearly, your Honour. Clearly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Now with respect to duress, however, it is your position that that is not justification. That is an excuse. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. AKHAVAN
utterances.text: It is an excuse, and even so we would submit it is not open to the crime of murder.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Okay. Is it your position that with respect to duress that when a person is acting under duress, they nevertheless have the mens rea and Actus Reus to commit the crime?

utterances.speaker: MR. AKHAVAN
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: They, however, are excused for what reason?

utterances.speaker: MR. AKHAVAN
utterances.text: They are excused, as I tried to explain, essentially for moral considerations for reasons of what society's expectations are of what a reasonable person should do in a situation of extreme pressure. I think that one has to make a distinction between a crime in the technical sense, a crime which involves mens rea and Actus Reus as distinct from the moral considerations surrounding that act. To say there was no moral choice is not say there was no mens rea. The accused who has a pistol pointing at his head who is asked to kill another person is entirely conscious of his act. He has the intent to kill another person. So the crime is unlike justification of self-defence not the same, and the reason why a particular jurisdiction may decide to exculpate such a person is entirely because of moral considerations, reasonable of public policy, societal expectations, whatever --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: I am sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: I was muttering to myself. I am sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: We are all very passionate up here. Go on.

utterances.speaker: MR. AKHAVAN
utterances.text: Perhaps I am mistaken but that is my understanding of the law. For that reason it would not in theory be any serious injustice to any accused to suggest this is not a crime of unlimited application -- I am sorry -- this is not a defence of unlimited application. Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: So if, therefore, the plea that was asserted was the plea of duress, and if it did not constitute a defence like self-defence a justification, was the plea equivocal and need it be remanded to the trial chamber?

utterances.speaker: MR. AKHAVAN
utterances.text: Clearly not, your Honour. We have made this submission in our brief that clearly since duress is not a defence to killing innocent human beings, and since the case involves the killing not only of one but of between 70 and 100 human beings by the admission of the accused, that clearly the plea was unequivocal in that duress, even if it was raised as a defence, which it was not, we submit, would not have been open to the accused, and I believe that we have included in our written brief authority by way of example from a US Court Martial, where the court held that the plea of guilty was unequivocal and was valid in view of the fact that duress was not open as a defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: The question that I now want to pose to you relates to the hypothetical regarding the hostage takers that the President referred to. I am not going to take you through all the As, the Bs and the Cs, but my question is really this: in the sentencing judgement the trial chamber 1 refers to an incident where the accused opposed the order of a Lieutenant Colonel to participate in the execution of 500 Muslim men. He was able not to commit this further crime because three of his comrades supported him when he refused to obey. So my question is: in a situation where you might have hostage takers is it not possible that if you refuse to obey that the in the process up might get some comrades who might also refuse to obey? We are speaking philosophically. Do you understand my question or is it just a comment?

utterances.speaker: MR. AKHAVAN
utterances.text: I think your question is exactly on point. Part of the philosophical occasion of the proportionality of evil is whether the law should require of people that they be heroes and martyrs or whether the law will permit one to be, if you like, a coward under the circumstances. The evil which is involved is not simply a numerical equation, as you point out. If the law permits duress as a defence, in a sense it may encourage such behaviour. It may allow people to submit to such pressure without fear of criminal culpability. As you have pointed out the case before us clearly indicates that when the accused did refuse, that this was supported by his colleagues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: It might not only encourage people to follow up your argument, but it might encourage them without justification, and I do not want to use that word "justification" when we are talking about self-defence, because the cases that I have read where a defence -- where duress has been recognised as a defence, it is rare -- I can think of one only but I am sure there are others -- where the accused was able to meet those very stringent requirements to establish that defence. What you are doing is saying there is a defence and following your argument encouraging or at least perhaps not discouraging an individual from being the first to say "no", and in the process what you really have in the application is a defence that very rarely succeeds because it is so very stringent. If we are talking philosophically and talking about upholding the rule of law and discouraging the perpetration particularly of crimes against humanity, it seems to me that that argument regarding mitigation as opposed to defence meets that concern you have expressed.

utterances.speaker: MR. AKHAVAN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Let me ask you this, though: is it your position that duress can never be accepted as a defence? I gather your answer would be no to that, that it can be accepted as a defence in certain circumstances?

utterances.speaker: MR. AKHAVAN
utterances.text: Clearly our position is duress is recognised in virtually every legal system in the world as a defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Let me interrupt you. Is it accepted as a defence to a violation of international and humanitarian law?

utterances.speaker: MR. AKHAVAN
utterances.text: Well, I believe that we have reduced our specific submission to the question of murder, because --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: I understand that. I have read your brief very carefully, but I want to ask you: is it your position that duress can be accepted as a defence to a violation of international humanitarian law, inhumane treatment?

utterances.speaker: MR. AKHAVAN
utterances.text: Once again by way of preliminary remarks I would submit that, yes, it can be admissible as a defence to certain crimes. There is a very big difference between, let us say, deportation or wanton destruction of property, and killing 100 people. One can clearly not by any standard of morality make any equation between those two crimes, but for the specific case before us we have only dealt with the question of murder. As I explained, for example, in the United Kingdom, other crimes such as, for example, sexual assault, can be excused based on the defence of duress, whereas in Canada it cannot. So this will be a problem for the court to determine at some future point in time. Where is the line to be drawn? What are the limits of duress as a defence? One could envisage murder, especially when it constitutes part of crimes against humanity, as being clearly among the most exceptionally serious crimes before this jurisdiction. So that, we would submit, would clearly fall within the area where duress should not apply as a defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: What is your position regarding the Secretary General's report at paragraph 57 that refers to coercion or lack of moral choice as a defence? Is it your position that he was referring generally to the existence of duress as a defence but not specifically focusing on the instance when a person takes the life of an innocent human being?

utterances.speaker: MR. AKHAVAN
utterances.text: I think it is a general proposition with which we would not disagree. The general principles of law recognise duress as an excuse. The International Law Commission's report also recognises duress as an excuse. But the paragraph 57 which you referred to actually is in relation to superior orders, I believe, in the report of the Secretary General, and I think the formulation, if I may say, is somewhat ambiguous. It is not clear what is actually being said there. One sees even in the post-second world war judgements that a lot of the cases dealt with duress in passing when dealing with superior orders. So of course one sees in Einsatzgruppen, High Command and other cases the court acknowledges that superior orders can never be a defence. In passing it says: "However, if accompanied by duress, it may be a defence". That is why I think maybe some of the decisions have not really reflected carefully on the law. They have just made a statement in passing by way of obiter dicta I think that the Secretary General's report concedes a point which we also concede, that duress is in general a defence, but when one goes beyond the general principle and looks at the particular application, the applicable case law suggests the contrary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: So what you are suggesting is that in this case we should focus on the issue of whether duress is a defence when it is accompanied by a superior order?

utterances.speaker: MR. AKHAVAN
utterances.text: You mean in paragraph 57 of the Secretary General's report?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Well, in your brief you say in 1.3: "With respect to duress accompanying superior orders, which is specifically at issue in the present case ...". Then you go on to say "the jurisprudence of the international military Tribunal at Nuremberg", etc., etc.

utterances.speaker: MR. AKHAVAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: In other words, is there a difference between how this Tribunal should treat a plea of duress if it involves the killing of an innocent human being, when that killing is not accompanied by a superior order?

utterances.speaker: MR. AKHAVAN
utterances.text: Clearly. Clearly the defence of duress, if it was raised in this case, was in conjunction with superior orders.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. AKHAVAN
utterances.text: We would submit that since superior orders categorically is not a defence under international law, and there is very little doubt of that point, that when it is combined with the defence of duress, that on the balance one should steer away from allowing that to be used as a defence. I am not prepared here to make any specific discussions as to what implications that may have on evidentiary standards and so on and so forth, but I think that duress, even when we are dealing with cases not involving murder, duress accompanying superior orders should only rarely -- I should say should be admitted even more rarely than duress as a general species should be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: But the issue before us is the question of whether duress accompanying superior orders should be a defence or mitigating circumstances. You are suggesting we focus on that issue and not decide in the abstract whether duress may be a defence in other circumstances; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. AKHAVAN
utterances.text: Well, your Honour, our position is that duress as such, irrespective of superior orders, can never be a defence to murder.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: So you are going to bite off more than you need to chew?

utterances.speaker: MR. AKHAVAN
utterances.text: Yes. We believe the case law supports that proposition.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. AKHAVAN
utterances.text: We are prepared to submit in addition that the accompanying superior orders makes it even more persuasive.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: On the question of proportionality, is it your position that the Tribunal should take into consideration the number of persons killed, the circumstances surrounding the killing of innocent persons, the position of the accused either in the military or even in the political structure? Is that something we should take into consideration in determining whether or not duress is a defence when it is accompanied by superior orders?

utterances.speaker: MR. AKHAVAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, that would not be necessary if duress is not a defence to murder. Then such an enquiry may only be taken into consideration in mitigation of punishment. Clearly if the accused killed one person to save ten POWs, the court may decide to give a very light sentence or to remit the sentence altogether as justice requires under the circumstances, but this may be even one of the reasons philosophically why duress should not be admitted as a defence to murder, because one immediately sees even from a philosophical point of view the immensely difficult balancing which a court would have to engage in in such a circumstance. It would be really a case of a numbers game, if you like, of: "Is it better to kill one person and save ten? Is it better to save one small child, let us say, as opposed to two elderly people? Is it better to save a lawyer as opposed to an accountant?" One could engage in all sorts of highly problematical philosophical discussions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Let me ask you a question regarding the report of the International Law Commission that you referred to earlier. In that report it states that: "The 1948 convention on genocide and the 1949 Geneva conventions and the most recent 1977 edition protocol 1 provides for no possible defences to those crimes". How does that affect the issue that the appeals chamber is faced with, if at all?

utterances.speaker: MR. AKHAVAN
utterances.text: Well, the issue of genocide is, I would say, somewhat different, because of the particular intent requirement of the crime of genocide, but I believe that -- I am not aware of this particular passage from the report of the international law commission, and I would like the opportunity to study it more carefully. Our position is not that, at least with respect to ordinary violations of humanitarian law as opposed to genocide, which is a different case, our position is not there are no defences whatsoever. I think that part of the problem in the deliberations of the International law Commission, of course, is that you have people coming from very different jurisdictions with very different understandings of what criminal responsibility entails, how defences relate. Our view is not that there are no defences whatsoever to violations of humanitarian law in general. So I would have to study more carefully that passage. I am somewhat surprised that there would be such a statement with the exception of the crime of genocide, where many commentators have suggested that even self-defence cannot be a justification for the crime of genocide.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Need the appeals chamber in the present case reach issue of whether superior orders is a defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. AKHAVAN
utterances.text: It does not need to because it is conclusively determined by Article 7.4 of the Statute. It can only be pleaded in mitigation of punishment and I think international law is decisive on that point. The only question is that of duress accompanying superior orders.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: What you are saying is that it is clear that it is not a defence but may only be used for mitigating circumstances. My question is: is it an issue? You are giving me the answer and what you are telling me is that it clearly can be used only for mitigating purposes and not a defence, but my question is; is that something that we should even decide?

utterances.speaker: MR. AKHAVAN
utterances.text: No, your Honour, it is not an issue at all in the present case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: I am going to defer to some other judges and come back.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: I had a couple of enquiries.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone please, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: First of all, you mentioned the decision in the Einsatzgruppen case was against US military law. I would be interested to know the details of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. AKHAVAN
utterances.text: I suppose that since there was no international precedent which the US Military Tribunal could rely on that the most expedient source of law for them would have been either US Military Law or US Common Law. I am unaware of any decision in US Military Law from 1896 up to the time of the Einsatzgruppen trial which would support the proposition. Perhaps I have not done my research as thoroughly as possible. The source I have relied on is Winthrop's Military Law and Precedents, which I understand to be, if you like, the bible of American Military Law. That source, which is reproduced in the book of authorities for you, indicates no case in which duress was admitted as a defence to murder. I believe that a line of cases from 1951 onwards in US court martials have specifically stated that duress is not a defence to murder. Of course, that is after the Einsatzgruppen decision, so I would not want to rely on that to speak about the state of the law in 1948 when the decision was made, but the consensus in general in US military law is clearly in support of our position. PRESIDENT CASSESE: But, again, I see a contradiction in what you are saying, because the Einsatzgruppen case is the only case where the American Military Tribunal sitting at Nuremberg applied Control Council Law Number 10. You insisted on this fact. You said some courts apply national law and others apply Control Council Law Number 10, but unlike the cases you have mentioned before American US court martials where US court martials applied US national law, in the Einsatzgruppen case Control Council Law Number 10 was applied. So therefore in a way you cannot put them on the same footing. Sorry to interrupt.

utterances.speaker: MR. AKHAVAN
utterances.text: No, your Honour. I think I should draw a distinction between Control Council Law Number 10 in terms of -- I made a distinction by saying that Control Council Law Number 10, like the Nuremberg Charter, may be considered as international law. I wish to make that distinction to say that the national courts in the occupied parts of Germany were operating as international courts as distinct from a decision such as Touvier or Priebke, and on and so forth, which may or may not borrow from international law, as it may be permitted to do, but clearly Control Council Law Number 10 did not involve an exhaustive penal code. It could not have. There were many uncertainties as to what were permissible defences. The same applies before this court, as we see today. The Statute is not exhaustive. So the court was left with limited options when Control Council Law Number 10 did not provide any guidance and international law could not provide any guidance. It could decide to rely on German law, on French law, an Anglo-American law. It could decide to do a survey of all legal systems. So there were many options available to it. Now my problem with the Einsatzgruppen decision, your Honour, is that the court cites no authority whatsoever. It seems to be one sentence which seems more like a sort of moral proposition. No court will find a man culpable if he pulls a lethal lever with a pistol loaded at his head. How much does that tell us about the legal reasoning behind that statement? As I said, in the context of a case dealing with the Einsatzgruppen execution squad, I think the court would have dealt with that in a way not spending any time, not giving it any credence. So in that sense the holding of the case is somewhat arbitrary. It is very well possible that based on one's moral conscience or one's common sense one could come to that conclusion. The judges sitting in that case may have said: "Clearly if someone has a pistol loaded and pointed at one's head, they should not be held guilty of killing others". Even if that is not the case, we will just mention it in passing. I would submit that statement in the Einsatzgruppen case is stated by way of obiter dicta. Even if it could be on point in that case, it was at no point seriously considered. The reason why we have relied so heavily on the Holzer, the Stalag Luft III case, the Furstein case is because the court considered at great length the issue. The issue was raised as a credible defence. This was not a case of extermination squads. One of them involved several defendants, up to ten or fifteen defendants, who had killed some fifty Royal Air Force Officers, who had been shot down and captured as prisoners of war. It is conceivable in those cases if duress was open as a defence to murder, that they may have had a defence. Therefore, the court considered that issue at great length. Having no clear international precedent, it relied on Archbold's Regina v Dudley and Stevens, and so on and so forth. But at this point in time one can make all sorts of hypothetical queries as to what may have happened, let us say, if that particular court sitting was a Chinese court applying Chinese law. Certainly the outcome may have been different. It is historical circumstance which has created that body of law. I do not think it is now open for us to question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Going back to this question of Einsatzgruppen being against US military law, I am right in thinking all you are saying there is not that military law says duress shall not be a defence in the case of murder, but rather you rely on what is said in Winthrop; is that so? You find no authority positive acceding to the proposition that duress is a defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. AKHAVAN
utterances.text: That is correct with respect to the US military law.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: That is what I am talking about. It was your remark, you see, that elicited this query. I wanted to then ask you: the passage that you cite from Winthrop does not seem to deal with it at all. It is dealing with compulsion of the enemy. It takes the view that such a defence can be sustained by proof of an immediate danger of death threatened by the enemy, which rather suggests that at least treason, which is compulsion, which is what is being discussed, is excusable when duress of that nature is exercised.

utterances.speaker: MR. AKHAVAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: That is as far as you can go on military law, is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. AKHAVAN
utterances.text: Yes. Clearly, your Honour, we are presupposing that were duress open as a defence to murder that it would have been stated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: I see.

utterances.speaker: MR. AKHAVAN
utterances.text: Because it is a crime of such exceptional gravity that it would not have been ignored in such a commentary. So the reason why we have cited that relevant passage is to say that the only crime which appears to be recognised as a defence -- I am sorry -- the only crime with respect to which duress can be a defence is that of treason.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Is treason.

utterances.speaker: MR. AKHAVAN
utterances.text: Of course the US military law cannot be considered in isolation from US law as a whole. We wanted to go through different stages in our analysis and say let us reduce it purely to a US military law since this was a US military Tribunal. They had no authority to rely on, none whatsoever. Then if one takes that analysis to the second stage of looking at US law, then we have the Orb versus State again before the Alabama courts I believe in 1893 and the subsequent case before the Rhode Island courts in 1904. Of course, we have would have made an exhaustive list of numerous other cases decided in the 1920s and 1930s that all repeat the proposition that duress is not a defence to murder.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: I gather it varies state to state in the United States subject to those states that have adopted the model penal code.

utterances.speaker: MR. AKHAVAN
utterances.text: My understanding, your Honour, is that generally duress is not admitted as a defence to murder and I believe that that is the law throughout the United States.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Throughout, you say.

utterances.speaker: MR. AKHAVAN
utterances.text: This is my understanding, but I do believe that there is legislation in certain states which allows for a partial defence such that murder may be reduced to manslaughter where duress is present. So in that sense one could say that it is recognised as a partial defence, but I am not aware of any state in the United States where either legislation or judicial opinion recognises a complete defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Thank you. The next question I wanted to ask you about is in the cases that you particularly rely on, Holzer and Furstein, it is what the Judge Advocate said to the Tribunal that you cite. We do not know at all what credence was given by the Tribunal to the Judge Advocate's argument, do we?

utterances.speaker: MR. AKHAVAN
utterances.text: No. This is the problem with many of these cases, some of which are not reported. I believe the Holzer trial is not -- I have not seen a copy of the Holzer trial anywhere except in the UN War Crimes Commission Report. I am sure President Cassese would be one of the few people in the world who would have a copy and would have may actually read through the whole decision as well. It is the passion for international law which I deeply appreciate, but my understanding is, first of all, in those cases the defence was not applied. It was never applied in any case, and that in itself should give us a certain indication, but my understanding is that the judge -- I would presume that the opinion of the Judge Advocate general would be applied by the court. I think that is a very reasonable assumption to make.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Was that a jury case, Holzer, and if it were a jury case, perhaps does that explain the result, that is the failure, absence of an explanation? At least in the United States the judge would typically charge the jury and you would have before you at least a charge as to what the law is and then the jury would apply the facts. I am not sure what the procedure is in Canada, but it being a jury case, can that perhaps explain why we would go to another source to look at a further explanation?

utterances.speaker: MR. AKHAVAN
utterances.text: Yes. I believe to the best of my knowledge that it is a variation of the jury system to the effect that the Judge Advocate General is actually instructing lay persons as to the applicable law. That gives me reason to believe that that is the applicable law which the court relied upon in arriving at its decision.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Thank you. Then does it come down in your view to this, and I look at the report of the International Law Commission in its 48th session in 1996, where it cites the Nuremberg Tribunal and concludes, after dealing first of all with the non-recognition of superior orders as a defence: "The true test which is found in varying degrees in the criminal law of most nations is not the existence of the order but whether moral choice was, in fact, possible". Is that in substance what you are putting and, if so, how do you apply it to the case where we have here, according to the accused's statement, that he was going to be shot together with the other ten if he did not obey the order? Where is the moral choice there?

utterances.speaker: MR. AKHAVAN
utterances.text: I would, first of all, say that that statement in the judgement of the international military Tribunal is somewhat ambiguous because they are speaking about superior orders. They say it is not a defence and then they say the true test is whether or not, in fact, moral choice -- it is not clear what they are saying. If we give it the benefit of doubt and suggest what they are saying is superior orders is not a defence but duress is or may be, even so, that does not at all change what we have already submitted. It is merely a recognition by the international military Tribunal that duress a species of defence which is accepted as such throughout the legal systems of the world, but the specific application of that defence is left entirely unanswered by the Tribunal. Now, the question of moral choice once again is a moral question. It does not go to the mens rea of the accused. It may be that I wilfully kill one person to save the life of ten people. Of course, I would be killing the accountant to save the lawyers, but this does not in any way mean that I did not have the requisite mens rea to commit the crime of murder with malice aforethought, premeditated. So that statement of the International Military Tribunal on moral choice does not change the fact that the accused committed the crime, in this particular case participating in the execution of some 1200 people over a five hour period, and that he possessed the requisite mens rea and the actus reus for crimes against humanity, but that because of the circumstances, and I am not going to comment here on what evidence is available to support those circumstances, but because of the circumstances the court may decide: "Well, he had no moral choice" or "his moral choice was limited" and that should be taken into consideration in mitigation of punishment up to and including the remission of the sentence. But moral choice -- I am not aware of any theory of criminal law which makes lack of moral choice as opposed to lack of mens rea a categorical defence to a crime.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: I see. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Judge Stephen, may I just follow up on that, because there is one sentence after that quote that perhaps might explain it. What Judge Stephen read is: "The true test which is found in varying degrees in the criminal law of most nations is not the existence of the order but whether moral choice was, in fact, possible". The next sentence reads, however: "Clearly an individual who was responsible in some measure for the existence or the execution of an order or whose participation exceeded the requirements thereof could not claim to have been deprived of a moral choice to his course of conduct". So I think that sentence has to be read with the previous sentence. The previous sentence raises a question. Then there is an answer which says that a person who executed that order could not claim that he was deprived of moral choice. Sorry. I just wanted to throw that in at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: It is not quoted for some reason in the 1996. Two questions that I had which may be ones directed to Mr. Niemann rather than to you. The first one is a puzzling passage in the sentencing judgement on page 9 at the top of the page. On that page it is said: "Although the accused did not challenge the manifestly illegal order he was allegedly given ...", and so on. That also appears in the French original, which I have checked. Is that an error, because the whole point of our discussion for the last couple of hours has been that the accused did challenge?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Well, your Honours, I think that) -- I do not know that there is any evidence to suggest that he did not challenge it at the time that he was given the order. I think that what -- I do not think there is any evidence there to say that when the order was given to him, he then immediately did more than simply say: "I am not -- I do not wish to commit this crime", and he was told: "Then you can line up". So I think that is the state of the evidence. But I am not sure that he went any further than that. It may be that what the sentencing court was looking at at that point was the references he made to the previous occasions, when he manifestly refused to simply carry it out and challenged the order to the full extent of refusal to carry it out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: I follow you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: It may be that is what is being referred to there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: The last thing I wanted to ask you about was the obligation when an accused is represented by counsel on the part of the court to state in detail the ingredients of the counts that are alleged. Here, of course, you had two alternative counts, a war crime or crime against humanity. Was there any obligation to state to an accused who was represented precisely what the elements of those two crimes are, the alternative crimes?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think when an accused is represented it is not an obligation of the court to do it. I think one of the points that I made earlier was that because after he said that he had pled guilty to the crime he did raise this question of saying: "I had to do it", I think the court was very anxious to ensures that he knew the full ambit of what was involved. I think in those circumstances it may be permissible, but I do not think it is mandatory or necessary. Any court confronted with a plea of guilty where an accused then says: "But I did it because I had to" would probably be approached to expand upon that in order to satisfy itself that the accused was, in fact, pleading guilty in order for it to accept the plea, because there is no question that the court is not obliged to accept the plea. So if the court is confronted with a plea that is equivocal, it may refuse or decline to accept it. What we say has happened here is that the issue was raised. The court then at great length went into it and satisfied itself that the plea was not equivocal and it could be accepted in the circumstances.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Thank you. PRESIDENT CASSESE: We have still five minutes. May I follow up on the question Judge Stephen has just raised? I have two questions. Now assuming your theory whereby duress cannot be urged as a defence in case of murder is right, so therefore it could only be urged as a mitigation, however it is a fact that it is apparent from what the defence lawyer has said in previous hearings as well as today that he in a way advised his client that duress might be urged either as a defence or as a mitigating circumstance. So he advised his client along those lines. So could one then infer from that that actually the client was wrongly advised and therefore his guilty plea was ambiguous, was inconsistent, because his defence lawyer was clearly under the influence of the Yugoslav law where, as I say, as he pointed out today repeatedly, duress can be urged both as a defence and as a mitigating circumstance, whereas if we were to stick to your view in international law duress could not have been invoked in this case as a defence but only as a mitigating circumstance? Now could we infer from that that therefore the guilty plea was invalid? I have a second question relating to this one. Again it is very clear from what the lawyer, defence counsel said to us today that he in a way wrongly advised his client on the issue of war crimes versus crimes against humanity. One could say -- I am not saying that he was wrongly advised, but I could say that one might argue that his client was wrongly advised because his client was not offered with a choice between war crimes or crimes against humanity. He was told: "Look, in this case because of the particular circumstances of the case, no war crime could be pleaded" or we could not accept any charge of war crime. The only crime which may be in issue is a crime against humanity. Therefore, could we argue because Mr. Erdemovic was wrongly advised when he chose to plead guilty to crimes against humanity, his plea was not valid and should be invalidated; his guilty plea should be invalidated?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Dealing with the first part of your Honour's question first, we would submit that even if counsel for the accused was mistaken, and I do not think we can assume that, then any ambiguity or uncertainty that may have existed was certainly put to rest by the remarks of the presiding judge in addressing the accused himself, and specifically addressing questions to the accused himself including the question: was he satisfied with his representation. In my submission, should there have been any difficulty there, then that was resolved clearly on the transcript. But, your Honours, I do not think that we should assume that this is an issue, because it certainly has not been raised by the Defendant, that he has been inadequately represented. Defence counsel may employ a number of strategies in how they may go about the process of representing their clients. It may be, and we are entitled to assume, that counsel for the defence was well aware of the position at common law. He was well aware of the position at international law. He was well aware of the Rules of the Tribunal and how this was being dealt with. He heard what the Presiding Judge had to say. He was aware of all those, but he may have chosen to still pursue the strategy which says: "Nevertheless, notwithstanding everything that has been said, this is the position that I am going to take on this matter". Now, it is pure speculation, in my submission, your Honour, on this matter to say perhaps it got it wrong or perhaps he did not understand. His position is stated. He presents it as two alternatives. It does not mean to say he did not know about the other alternative, and that is to say the law that was to be applied and the law the sentencing judge said he was going to apply. Dealing with the question of advice, I am afraid I cannot assist your Honour with that, other than to say I can only assume that the advice that he gave to his client was correct and again I emphasise that it has not been brought into question here by the accused and certainly not by his counsel. So in my submission, your Honour, it is very difficult for the Prosecution to respond to this in circumstances where it is not an issue that is being raised on the appeal, and it is merely a hypothetical question which we may pose as a result of some answers that have been given to certain questions, but there is nothing, your Honour, to suggest that Mr. Erdemovic has not been adequately, properly and fully represented in these proceedings from beginning to end, and that that adequate representation continues to now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Just on this point, it seems to me that the Trial Chamber 1 agreed with the position that Mr. Babic has taken, and that is that duress may be both a defence and a mitigating circumstance, if I understand the sentencing memorandum correctly. So if that is what Mr. Babic advised his client, at least as far as the Trial Chamber is concerned, that Trial Chamber agreed with him, the way that I read the sentencing memorandum.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: That certainly seems to be the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: If we were to remand this case -- I will ask this of Mr. Babic as well as you, Mr. Niemann -- should it be remanded to the Trial Chamber consisting of the same judges who imposed the sentence?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I would not have thought that was necessary, your Honour. It is certainly an option that is available to the court, but I do not think that there is anything to suggest that that has to be the case. I would think, however, that considerations of who confirmed the indictment and other such matters might need to be taken into account, but I do not know of any principle that says it has to go back before the exact same judges to be determined.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: My question is not must it but should it. I will ask Mr. Babic that question. Maybe it is Mr. Babic that should respond. PRESIDENT CASSESE: Mr. Babic?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Mr. Babic, if the Appeals Chamber were to remand this case back to the trial chamber should it appropriately remand it to the Trial Chamber consisting of the same judges who sentenced?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. BABIC
utterances.text: Throughout the proceedings I had absolutely no remarks regarding the course of the proceedings. I have no special reason, therefore, if this distinguished chamber were to decide to remand the case for retrial not to do so to the same Trial Chamber that passed the first judgement. Therefore, I have no objections in the case of this case being remanded for retrial that it go back to the same Trial Chamber. PRESIDENT CASSESE: Thank you. Before -- sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I am sorry, your Honours. There was just a couple of matters I wonder if I could very quickly clear up, because it was raised, and I fear it might be important. Your Honour, the reference to the word "acquitted" as it appears in the transcript in the English version in our submission it does not bear the same meaning in different languages. We have had that word checked some considerable time ago. Our advice from the translation people is the word used was a Serbian term and if I can perhaps try and pronounce it, "oslobodjenje od kazne", and I am informed, your Honours, that does not mean "acquitted" as the term is understood in the English language. In fact, it means discharge from punishment. So in our submission, your Honours, it can be misleading if great emphasis is put on that word "acquitted" and we would submit it is a mistake as appears as such. . I think there was only one other matter I would seek to clear up quickly, if I may, your Honour. That is that when I spoke of the question of whether or not he was concerned for his own life, and your Honour was curious about my comment on that, I simply make reference to the transcript, and I will just give your Honours reference to it, if I may, the transcript of 19th November 1996, page 36, line 1 he speaks of the possibility of escaping if it had not been for his wife and child. Also a reference on 19th November 1996, page 40, line 18. Just concluding that, your Honours, it is our submission that his wife and child was nowhere present at the time. So there was no immediacy at all in the suggestion he raised. PRESIDENT CASSESE: Mr. Babic, would you like to add a few things?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please. Microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. BABIC
utterances.text: May I please explain my position a little further? Our positions regarding the plea of guilt are not in opposition against one another, because when sentence is passed according to the Yugoslav Criminal Code and the law on criminal proceedings, which is modelled on the French criminal law, the sentence is passed in such a way that the accused is proclaimed guilty for the commission of such and such an act and after that he may be discharged from punishment for such and such reasons. Therefore, the plea of guilt remains. It is verified, but the punishment is not carried out, because of certain reasons. That is one point. Secondly, I think that our positions regarding duress and the way in which it is dealt with in national legislations and the repercussions it has on international criminal law do not differ also. It is either accepted as defence or as mitigating circumstance. The only question is whether this specific case is such as to require relief from responsibility or is it just a mitigating circumstance. Of course, that is up to the honourable judges to decide. Regarding the question of moral choice and orders, I have tried to elaborate that in my brief and I wish to avoid all repetition, but I think that moral choice in this specific case and in the concrete circumstances as described by the accused Erdemovic, and we have no other description of the act nor the circumstances surrounding it, except that given by Erdemovic, we cannot avoid but conclude that the accused had no other moral choice, and when we are talking about the equivalence of principles, what is the equivalence? All those innocent Muslims, on the one hand, plus one Erdemovic, or was it just that those 1,000 Muslims minus one Erdemovic, be he hero or not? So if we had Erdemovic executed as well, which would be inevitable, or in this case he made a different choice. Actually he sacrificed his own dignity at that moment in the interest of saving his life. What he stated here and before the Yugoslav authorities, that is that he wanted to go for trial and he told the Yugoslav authorities: "Yes, I participated in that execution" and that was the same statement that he made here at his initial appearance. That is obviously probably his unconscious attempt to explain his position at the time of the commission of the crime. I think that this distinguished chamber has many elements and facts at its disposal as the first instance in international criminal law to provide a precise answer regarding the responsibility of an ordinary soldier when committing a criminal offence under superior orders, and that also in that context the question of coercion, extreme necessity and superior orders in such cases. Also the question has been raised whether I gave the wrong advice to my client. A war crime and a crime against humanity are treated in the Statute as the same criminal offences. When we had to take a decision, President Jorda asked which of these offences we opted for. At that point it seemed to us the same, because the gravity of the offences were equal, but the grounds were different, and that is what determined our choice. Thirdly, according to Yugoslav law, and I repeat it is modelled on the criminal proceedings of France, the court is not bound to the legal qualification given by the Prosecution or the defence. The Trial Chamber can itself characterise a certain act and draw conclusion on guilt or innocence at its own discretion. Those would be my additional comments, your Honours. PRESIDENT CASSESE: Thank you very much indeed. Since it is late --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: I have a question that goes to the preliminary question, and that is in order to be found guilty of a crime against humanity certain nexus has to be established. Either Mr. Niemann or Mr. Akhavan. If an individual acts under duress, can it be said that he is acting for purely personal reasons and thus the elements would not have been met, or do you want to answer this after lunch?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Perhaps I might answer it after lunch.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Okay. PRESIDENT CASSESE: So we adjourn until 2.45. (1.10 pm) (Luncheon adjournment) (2.45 pm) PRESIDENT CASSESE: Good afternoon. I apologise for the slight delay. It is my fault. We now go on with questions to the prosecutor. Judge McDonald?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I had a question which I promised to deal with at the resumption this afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: I am sure I have a very good answer. You had, what, an hour and a half to think about it?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honour, on the question of intent in the context of duress, where duress is raised, it is our submission that the issue is not the distinction so much between a crime against humanity and a war crime but between an international crime against humanity and a domestic crime. Perhaps if I could assist by giving an example. Assume, for example, that a German soldier during World War II at a bar participates in a drunken brawl and he is insulted and as a consequence of that he then proceeds to murder somebody. In our submission, if it is later subsequently found out that that person happened to be a Jewish person, that does not make the crime a crime against humanity or, in our submission, a war crime, nor in our submission should one's motives be conclusive as to why a person participates in a crime. In our submission, on the facts of this case there can be no question that the crime involved is a widespread or systematic attack against a civilian population. In our submission there is no question that the accused knew this at the time that he participated in this event. In our submission there is no question that the accused formed the intent to kill these persons knowing full well of the broader context in which his acts occurred, and that he knew of these broader contexts. Indeed, it is our submission that the actual number of killing of people just in this one incident would be sufficient to satisfy the criteria of widespread or systematic, but there is no reason to assume that he did not have a broader knowledge than that, having regard to his participation in the events of the war, and in particular having regard to the fact that he had participated in effect on armies on both sides of this particular conflict. Your Honours, even if he did have purely personal reasons for participating in the commission of a crime, it is our submission that the fact that he may himself have had personal reasons for doing something does not of itself exclude the fact that he intended to participate in a widespread and systematic attack such as to make it a crime against humanity. So it is our submission that the facts of the case are very instructive as to the circumstances in which this accused found himself and the state of knowledge that he had. In our submission, your Honours, there could be no doubt that he knew that he was participating in this broader context when he committed these murders.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Thank you. PRESIDENT CASSESE: Any further questions?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: No. PRESIDENT CASSESE: All right. We might move on to the merits, but before we do so, may I just pick up a point which has been raised this morning by Judge Stephen concerning the Holzer case? Actually I happened to get from the Canadian authorities the record of proceedings and I would just like to tell you in a few minutes the facts of the case. There were three German members of the Wermacht, the German army, who killed one of three Canadian airmen who had been taken prisoner. Two Germans participated in the killing of the Canadian and both of them pleaded not only superior order but also duress, and one of them said, and I am quoting from the proceedings: "The Lieutenant pulled his pistol, held it against me and said: "Do you want to or don't you want to?"" Then he had to kill. There I think Mr. Akhavan is right in saying that actually it is clear from the whole case that duress was rejected as a defence because both the Prosecutor and the Judge Advocate excluded the vocation of duress for the killing of an innocent person, and actually the court sentenced the two men to death, while the third German, who had not participated in the killing, was sentenced to 15 years' imprisonment. So much for the case, but again I would like to -- the reason why I mentioned the facts of this case is that again we are here in one of these situations which I mentioned this morning, namely again a Lieutenant menacing two people, two soldiers, to kill them if they did not execute the airman. So for each of them the choice was between his own life and the life of a POW. So, therefore, it is quite different from the situation to which I tried to draw your attention this morning, where in any case the person under duress knows that the people to be killed will be killed whatever his own position.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: It is a very difficult issue, especially when a gun is being held at one's head. All I can say, your Honour, is that this was an issue that was looked at. Specifically that sort of scenario was looked at by the House of Lords in Abbott's case, the one I quoted from at length. Indeed, that is the argument that was advanced by the defence counsel in that case. The defence counsel in that case says: "This calls for heroism which exceeds anything which should be required of ordinary human beings in the circumstances of the modern environment". When his Lordship, Lord Salmon, was addressing the problem, he specifically referred to a hypothetical situation where it was a person who was forced to commit the crime, where he knew that he and his family would be killed for failure to do so. Yet, notwithstanding that, the House of Lords said that it was still contrary to the law of England and it could not be contemplated to be part of the law of England that the killing of an innocent human being could be a justification -- duress involving a crime which involved the killing of a human being could be admitted in these circumstances. So the House of Lords, if it is of any assistance to your Honours, did actually consider that very fact scenario that your Honour raised and, notwithstanding it, rejected it, but that is the only authority that I can refer your Honour to but it was certainly considered in that case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: May I ask this one question as a follow-up? It seems to me that if we begin to discuss this whole notion of whether someone should be required to give up their life rather than take another life, and if we come to the conclusion that -- the transcript is not working, is it? Let us wait a moment. (Pause.) I will withdraw my question. I think that was a sign, that the transcript stopped working.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I think it stopped before that, your Honour. I just hope it is not necessary to repeat everything I have said. PRESIDENT CASSESE: I think we have come to an end of our discussion of the preliminary issues raised by the Appeals Chamber in its Order. We can now move on to what I would term the merits of the appeal. I wonder whether the defence counsel and the Prosecutor have anything to add to their written briefs. If this is so, then I would like to ask them to confine themselves to ten minutes each. Mr. Babic, have you anything to add to what you wrote in your written submission?

utterances.speaker: MR. BABIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, what I have written and what I have said today, I do not have anything much to add to that. One question that arose from our discussion here today is the issue of the principle of reformatio in pjus if it comes to the remand of this case. If such a decision were to be made by this Chamber, then we would have to also obey the principle of reformatio in pjus, that it cannot be any worse for the accused. PRESIDENT CASSESE: Thank you. You know, it is not a question of reformatio in pjus, P-J-U-S. Why? Because again if the Appeals Chamber decides, if it were to decide to remand the case to the Trial Chamber, there would be a proper trial. So, therefore -- not a sentencing procedure, a proper trial. Then, of course, it would be for the Trial Chamber to decide whether the accused is guilty or innocent, and if he is found guilty what sort of sentence he should be given. So, therefore, I do not see any question of reformatio in pjus. Normally the question of reformatio in pjus arises with regard to any sentence passed by the Appeals Chamber. Is that clear to you?

utterances.speaker: MR. BABIC
utterances.text: Absolutely clear. I just wanted you to bear this principle in mind in some way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: I wonder -- with the disadvantage of a Common Law background, that Latin tag and its meaning is not clear to me. Would you like to translate "reformatio in pjus"?

utterances.speaker: MR. BABIC
utterances.text: According to the Yugoslav Criminal Code and the law on criminal procedure and according to the European laws and criminal procedure, when the accused is appealing the judgement, if the case is retried, the sentence handed down cannot be more serious, nor can his offence be classified as more serious. This is the essence of the principle of reformatio in pjus.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Thank you. PRESIDENT CASSESE: I understand that you do not have anything to add except for what you just said to your --

utterances.speaker: MR. BABIC
utterances.text: No. PRESIDENT CASSESE: I wonder whether the Prosecutor has anything to add to his written Respondent brief?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Just very shortly, your Honour, yes. Your Honours, just dealing with the --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And it is relating to what might happen, depending on the decision of the Appeals Chamber, I just note that in Article 25 of the Statute of the Tribunal the authority given to the Appeals Chamber is to affirm, reverse or revise the decision taken by the trial chambers. So if the matter was to be remitted back, it would have to be somewhere in the context of that, I would imagine, but it is not specifically spelt out, but that is an authority of the Appeals Chamber. The only other matter that I wish to draw your Honours' attention to is this, that it is not, in our submission, appropriate to argue that it is somehow an error of law or fact that when a party to a proceedings advances a particular point of view, and in this case in our submission particularly duress as mitigation, to then say that the Trial Chamber or the sentencing Chamber failed or erred because it did not pick up that point and then call for further evidence at the time. It is up to the parties to persuade the sentencing Chamber that there are grounds for mitigation. If a party fills to do that, then that does not, in our submission, give rise to an appeal. So the burden is carried by the party to do that. Now in the context of the trial obviously if a defence is raised obviously the burden rests on the Prosecution to carry it from the beginning to the end. The Prosecution must prove beyond a reasonable doubt that the person did not come within the terms of that defence, for example, self-defence, that the person did not act in self-defence. The Prosecution carries that burden. Once one reaches the stage where there is a plea of guilty or indeed a verdict entered and the accused is convicted, then if the defence wish to raise matters in mitigation, then the defence carries that responsibility to convince the court on the balance of probabilities that they were acting in circumstances that would justify mitigation of the penalty. In our submission the Prosecution is entitled to refute that or to call evidence to suggest that that is not the case, but it does not remove from the fact that the party that advances that proposition at that particular point in the proceedings carries that responsibility. It cannot assist the party to subsequently appeal if there is further evidence that could have been called or other submissions that could have been made which would have convinced the Chamber that those circumstances existed. Your Honours, finally, and although I feel it is probably a matter that the Chamber is fully aware of, having regard to our submissions, it is our submission that, of course, mitigation of the penalty can amount to the various matters that have been raised by counsel for the defence in the sense that no penalty at all can be imposed in terms of any prison sentence, so that if it is being suggested by counsel for the defence in the course of his submissions that what he is, in fact, seeking is a mitigation of the penalty to the point where no sentence in terms of a prison sentence is imposed, then, of course, that is available to the court at the time. He failed to do that in the circumstances of this case, but in our submission that does not detract from the fact that that was available to be argued and was available to be applied by the court. The court could have said: "We impose no prison sentence". Unless there are any other matters, those are our submissions, your Honour. PRESIDENT CASSESE: Thank you. If you do not mind, on the first point you made concerning Article 25 of our Statute, Article 25 (2), you are right, but may I draw your attention to rule 117C: "In appropriate circumstances the Appeals Chamber may order that the accused be retried according to law". So it is covered by our Statute, by our rules of procedure.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. PRESIDENT CASSESE: Thank you. I wonder whether there are any questions from judges? No questions on the merits. Judge McDonald?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: I have a few questions, some to both counsel. Let me ask you first, Mr. Babic, if I may. Is it your position that Mr. Erdemovic lacked the mental capacity or that there was diminished mental capacity at the time that the offence was committed or offences were committed by him?

utterances.speaker: MR. BABIC
utterances.text: I presented this position in the appellant's brief and in the appeal. In the absence of a competent evaluation of experts from forensic psychiatry, I could not have been as categorical as I wanted to be, although I did submit that he was at least in a state of diminished mental responsibility. I did not want to go that far as to say that he lacked mental responsibility, because I did not have appropriate medical evaluation to be able to make such a categorical statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: The Trial Chamber found that one of the mitigating circumstances refers to, and I will quote: " ... is the state of mental incompetence claimed by the defence". That is at page 46, paragraph 86, I believe. Now I read that as saying that the Trial Chamber was determining that one of the mitigating circumstances was the mental capacity of the accused when he committed the offence. The report that was requested, the examination of the accused was requested by the Trial Chamber, but the Trial Chamber did not ask, I gather, the psychiatrists and psychologists to answer that question, and that was what was the accused's mental state at the time. Yet the Trial Chamber rejects this. It says that is one of the mitigating circumstances, but seemingly concludes that there has been no showing that the accused even suffered from diminished mental capacity at the time that the offence was committed. So my question is: was it incumbent upon the Trial Chamber to include in its request of the psychiatrists and the psychologists when they examined the accused that that question be answered as well as the other ones that they asked, and I believe that is the position that you take in your brief, or was that option not open to you, that is you could also have requested that that question be put to the psychiatrists and the psychologists. So the question is: whose responsibility is it? What is the effect of the failure of the psychiatrists and the psychologists to reach a conclusion on this question, since it was not asked, considering that the Trial Chamber finds that one of the mitigating circumstances was the mental competence at the time that the offences were committed, yet no psychiatrist or psychologist was asked and, of course, they did not comment on that issue. So what effect, if any, does that have on the whole proceedings, including the plea as well as the sentence?

utterances.speaker: MR. BABIC
utterances.text: As for the psychiatrists, I cannot lay the blame on them for failing to respond to this question. The psychiatrists and the psychologists responded to the questions that the Trial Chamber asked. As for whether this question was raised at all during the trial, this question put in this precise manner was not asked by the Prosecutor, by the defence and by the Trial Chamber, so that we did not receive an answer.
