It was my opinion on the basis of the elements presented by the psychiatrists and the psychologists that I have enough foundation to make a legal conclusion that we were dealing with diminished mental capacity, and I presented that as a mitigating circumstance. I now propose that additional examination by experts be conducted, but I must say in this context that during the break in today's proceedings I explained to my client what the quashing of the first instance judgement would mean, and my client is absolutely opposed to another proceedings, he says that he could simply not bear that. He wants to know what his fate will be, even if it means that all this that I have said so far be considered as advocating mitigating circumstances and that these circumstances are such that a reduced sentence could be imposed. I refer now to a minimum sentence which is imposable according to the Yugoslav Criminal Code, and that is the sentence of five years' imprisonment. I think that if we take all these circumstances into account altogether, I think that they are so special, so peculiar, that I think that even this Trial Chamber could make a decision to that effect. Of course, that decision as regards the punishment could be changed. This is against my will, because I still advocate the legal and factual points, but since I have been mandated by my client, I have to present this before this Trial Chamber. PRESIDENT CASSESE: Thank you. I wonder whether the Prosecutor -- sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: I need to understand what you have just said. I thought you were going to comment on that. I do not know that I fully understand, Mr. Babic. Let me see if I can repeat to you what I understand. Are you saying that Mr. Erdemovic has been sentenced to ten years and that there has now been an appeal, but does he wish to go forward with this appeal, recognising the fact that this case may be reversed and remanded and that either the Trial Chamber could ask the accused to re-plead or perhaps there would be a trial, and in either circumstances unless the Trial Chamber considered itself bound to the principle that you just stated in Latin and then you kindly translated for us, your client may incur a heavier penalty, and are you now saying that that is something that your client has told you that he does not want to face, and what does that mean therefore with respect to this appeal? Maybe I misunderstood you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BABIC
utterances.text: My client has asked me and he requested, despite the fact that I have drawn his attention to the possible consequences of all this, he asked me to request from this Trial Chamber not to reverse and remand this case for retrial. He thought that this Chamber should once again consider all these facts that I presented and to re-evaluate all the mitigating circumstances and our opinion is that it is possible to take this appeal into account and to reduce his sentence. PRESIDENT CASSESE: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: I wonder if I can tell you what I understand you to be saying and see if you agree with me. Your client has instructed you that he does not wish to have a trial as a result of a not guilty plea being entered, but he would wish to have this court consider the sentence that has been imposed and presumably to consider the reduction of it. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. BABIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: If the Chamber were to determine that duress is a defence and not a mitigating circumstance, it may be then that the Appeals Chamber would have to determine therefore that the plea was equivocal and would therefore have to return it to the Trial Chamber, and at that point it would be up to the accused to decide whether he wished to enter a plea of guilty again, or go forward with a trial. Now you have said he would not want to go forward with a trial, but if this Appeals Chamber were to determine this were a defence, our conclusion would be that you cannot plead guilty if you continue to assert your plea of duress, and I hope he understands that. He would then -- I do not want to get too much further. It is hard enough trying to be a judge; I do not want to try to be a lawyer as well. That is what you are considering. If we can move beyond that, let me ask you another question, though, and that is that apparently the Trial Chamber at page 47 rejected the plea of duress of the accused because it found that it will require corroboration of his statements by independent evidence. What is your position regarding that? We do not have any rules of procedure that require corroboration and a trial Chamber has just issued an opinion and judgement finding that corroboration is not required, independent corroboration is not required, but apparently at least from reading Trial Chamber 1's decision or judgement, it finds that they reject -- it rejects his statement regarding duress because there was no corroboration. Seemingly the Trial Chamber accepts his testimony regarding the commission of the offences because they had evidence that it received during the Rule 61 proceeding, but the rule 61 proceeding is a proceeding where persons testify without being subjected to cross-examination. So for whatever value it was, the Trial Chamber accepted a portion of the accused's testimony but rejected his plea of duress because it said at least that there was no corroboration. What is your position regarding that?

utterances.speaker: MR. BABIC
utterances.text: My position has been stated before to this effect. The Trial Chamber evaluated the statements given by the accused Erdemovic in two manners. In places where his statement was evidence for the commission of the offence it was accepted by the Trial Chamber and in parts where the statement of the accused Erdemovic was his defence, it was not accepted, not only as defence but also as mitigating circumstance, and also in this case again they did not treat the rest as a mitigating circumstance. This is why I say that all this that the foundation on which I have built the case for duress, if I am to accept the position of my client, which I have to, I would ask this Chamber to accept this as a mitigating circumstance and to reduce the sentence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Mr. Niemann, would you respond to that question?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. Your Honours, in our submission what the Trial Chamber was doing when it went into this question of corroboration was that it was wearing its Tribunal fact hat and was not dealing with it as a matter of law. In our submission what the Chamber, the sentencing Chamber was expressing here, is acceptance or non-acceptance of the question of fact. What it is saying is: "We were not persuaded, we were not convinced, as a jury might, but we do not hear the reasons for a jury. We were not persuaded or convinced this was made out on the basis of the evidence that has been presented to us. As a consequence of that there was no corroboration of it or supporting evidence". In our submission, it is not the use of the technical term "corroboration" as it is understood in some jurisdictions. In our submission it is merely the evidence itself was not strong enough to persuade them as a Tribunal of fact that they had been persuaded, and they expressed their reasons for coming to that factual conclusion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: That is not what the Trial Chamber says in paragraph 91. Let us see. I may have the wrong one. It is on page 47. Let me see if I can find it. It is page 48. It is paragraph 91 on page 48: "The defence has produced no testimony, evaluation or other elements to corroborate what the accused has said. For this reason the judges deem that they are unable to accept the plea of extreme necessity". So I really have two points. One, if the Trial Court does not explain its basis for reaching a conclusion, it is very difficult for an Appellate Court to evaluate the correctness or the soundness of its decision. So if the Trial Chamber was not explaining itself, it puts us in a very difficult situation because we do not know why they reject it. Typically trial chambers would say: "Well, we have assessed credibility and we believe him" or whatever, but the only thing that is said is "they produced no testimony, evaluation or other elements to corroborate what the accused has said". It seems to me if that is what the Trial Chamber was looking for, it may have made an error of law, if there is no corroboration required in trials before this Trial Chamber, and so that is really my enquiry.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, I understand your Honour's point, but in my submission, your Honour, the situation is really no different to where one finds themselves in the context of a jury trial, where we never know what motivates a jury to decide one way or the other. If there was a clear statement, and I submit that I do not think it is clear, but if there was a clear statement which said: "As a matter of law we require corroboration and we instruct ourselves accordingly that in the determination of this question of fact that corroboration is a requirement and we are satisfied that that matter of law has not been established", then I would say yes, there is a problem, because even though the rules of the Tribunal in terms of evidence are very wide and broad, I think there does become a serious question whether evidentiary requirements such as corroboration can be imported in. I think there is an argument that that should not perhaps happen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: You say there is an argument what should have happened?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: You should not import evidentiary requirements of law such as corroboration in those circumstances. It would certainly be an arguable point that that is an error of law, but I am submitting, your Honour, that that is not the case here. I am suggesting to your Honours that the word "corroboration" used in the context in which it appears is really an expression of satisfaction of the state of the evidence. Just as a jury might do the same thing but not tell us why, it is the same issue, and that is: "This point has been raised but we have not been convinced. There is no corroboration. There is no other supporting material to suggest that this is the case and we have not been persuaded by the evidence". That is, in my submission, the context in which it has been raised. I say that in particular because when looking at paragraph 87 which also deals with that, your Honours, first of all, say, before it analyses mitigating circumstances: "The Trial Chamber wishes to recall sub-rule 89C of this Rule, which says it may admit any relevant evidence which it deems to have probative value. In respect of this the Trial Chamber will require the corroboration of the accused's statement by independent evidence". In my submission that is dealing with the question of admissibility of evidence and those matters that go to convince the Chamber of a particular point that has been raised by a party in the proceedings. I can go further, your Honours, and say there is a difference of approach between some jurisdictions between what is corroboration in its technical meaning. I mean, there are some jurisdictions that say, for example, that you cannot proceed to a conviction on a confession or a plea of guilty alone. There needs to be further evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could you please slow down?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Further evidence is referred to as corroboration, but it is not strict corroboration.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: They want you to be slower.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: It is not strictly corroboration in the same way as that term is understood as a strict evidentiary requirement as it is in some Common Law jurisdictions. So, in my submission, their Honours have not erred. They have not introduced a new rule of evidence that must be satisfied. They have merely expressed themselves as to why they have reached a conclusion of fact. PRESIDENT CASSESE: If I may raise an issue which does not relate specifically to this question of corroboration, but still to the question of whether or not evidence was produced to the effect that the Defendant acted under duress, I would like to have your views on the fact that actually the Trial Chamber discussed the matter of whether or not evidence had been provided on this point in the section on the validity of the guilty plea. I am referring to paragraph 20 of the Trial Chamber's sentence. Would you feel that in a way here the Trial Chamber dealt with an issue which is a typical issue for a Trial Chamber proceeding in a trial proper, and not in a sentencing proceeding? The issue whether or not evidence has been produced by defence counsel to the effect that the Defendant acted under duress, would you not feel that this was a proper matter for a trial, not for a sentencing proceeding, so that in this case actually, while considering the question of a guilty plea, actually the Trial Chamber behaved as a Trial Chamber conducting a trial?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honours, there is some element of the judges in the sentencing court perhaps importing into the procedures that they followed some aspects of the procedures that apply in their domestic jurisdictions. I must say that that is a fault that all of us suffer from from time to time, that we tend to look back upon our own jurisdictions. I think there is an aspect of that, and particularly when the court went on to determine the issue of whether or not duress was a defence or not. Perhaps it did not go that far, and perhaps that is not an appropriate course to be followed or perhaps it is. I do not know that there is any precise prescription as to how a court should handle a plea of guilty. I myself in my submissions have made reference to a decision in the United States and to one in England where -- particularly the one in the United States -- where the accused said: "I am not guilty of this offence" and the judge specifically said: "Do you plead guilty or not guilty?", and the accused said: "I am not guilty of this offence", but nevertheless the Supreme Court of the United States found that was not equivocal, that was appropriate and did not interfere with the resulting decision that followed. It seems to me, your Honours, that there is one understanding of how these matters should be dealt with, but when confronted with what might be or appear to be an equivocal plea, one can understand why a sentencing court may wish to explore and go further into the matter in order to satisfy itself whether or not the plea ought to be accepted in the circumstances. In my submission mostly this is what occurred in these proceedings. The sentencing court was very careful, was very concerned about the situation and wanted to be satisfied. It did go a little further than what some jurisdictions would go, but in my submission that does not give rise to an error of law which would justify the interference in the decision by this Chamber, in my respectful submission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: The American case you refer to is Elford's case, is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: If, of course, the plea of duress, though, is a defence, then, of course, the accused would be entitled to a trial on that. That is not something that could be resolved by way of a plea of guilty. It is your position that it may only be used for mitigation purposes. So, therefore, there was no error.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I am searching for my materials here, but there is also another case in the United States, which I could refer to and I will find the reference to in a moment, where the court was satisfied that the accused was insane at the time of the commission of the crime, yet he pleaded guilty, and even though on no understanding of the law as it then applied, the court held that nevertheless the plea was validly entered and could be accepted. I also made reference to the decision of Sullivan in the House of Lords in England, where although the court itself did not deal with this issue of an equivocal plea, what it was dealing with was the circumstances where a person had raised the issue of it. It had been found that he was insane and he immediately entered a plea of guilty. The matter went on appeal to the House of Lords and the House of Lords did not see fit to interfere with it, even though it had been established that the accused could not have been guilty of the crime in that sense, because he technically had a defence. All the rationale for all of this is there are times when although it may appear obvious that defences are available, that a party may elect to take a course of action which on some assessment may seem to be inappropriate. For example, in the case of Elford, the accused took the course he did because he feared the imposition of the death penalty. In the case of Sullivan he took the course he did because he was an epileptic and did not want to have the stigma of being insane. Those courses were taken and the courts saw fit not to interfere. In our submission, the principle is the same. There are fact situations which may differ, but in our submission that principle applies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Just one other question. What is the effect of the Trial Chamber erroneously, according to the defence, finding that the accused participated in the execution of 500 Muslims at -- what was the building? Pilica building? The accused has argued that the Trial Chamber made an error of fact and perhaps it infected its finding as far as mitigation or defence, however it was proceeding, because it erroneously concluded that he had participated in that execution, whereas, in fact, he had not. If it is an error, is it a serious enough error for this Appeals Chamber to reverse and remand and give the Trial Chamber an opportunity to reconsider its sentence in light of the true facts?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Well, in our submission, your Honour, we deal with this in particular in our written brief. In our submission, we still maintain the same position that the court was dealing with the question in terms of the overall factual situation of the events that occurred, but we submit there is nothing there to suggest that they considered that he had participated in the killing of the 500, and that they took that into account when they imposed the sentence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Mr. Babic, do you wish to comment on that point? Do you understand my question? The question is whether or not even though the Trial Chamber says that -- it concludes that the accused participated in the killing of the 500 Muslims, that really that did not play a part in its sentence, I guess. That is the position of the Prosecutor. What is your position?

utterances.speaker: MR. BABIC
utterances.text: I, too, wish to repeat the position I took in my brief on page 3 of the Serbo-Croatian text, in which I allege that such a statement on the part of the court necessarily reflected upon the sentence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Is it serious enough so that the Appeals Chamber should reverse it? Is it what is called reversible error or is it just a mistake they made that you have really not addressed?

utterances.speaker: MR. BABIC
utterances.text: I think it is not of such a magnitude that it cannot be corrected, and that this Appellate Chamber can put it right by the mitigation of the sentence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: One question arising out of that: is it not the fact that the Appellate Chamber merely said that the unit to which the accused belonged took part in the killing of 500 in the hall, not that the accused did? That is so, is it not?

utterances.speaker: MR. BABIC
utterances.text: Not even the unit. The 10th Sabotage detachment did not participate in that. Another unit did. That is why we are contesting the whole matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Yes, I realise that, but your complaint is only that the Trial Chamber said that the 10th Sabotage Unit did the killing of the 500, not that the accused did the killing of the 500. That is so, is it not?

utterances.speaker: MR. BABIC
utterances.text: The accused belonged to the 10 Sabotage detachment. This detachment has several units. On that day there was a certain squad, to which the accused belonged. Out of the eight of them, not one participated in the killing of 500 Muslims in Pilica, and therefore Erdemovic did not either. That is why I contested this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. PRESIDENT CASSESE: I wonder whether the parties would like to add anything? Mr. Babic, would you like to add anything before we wind up our hearing?

utterances.speaker: MR. BABIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, Mr. President, I must say that against my will I appeal to this Chamber to take into consideration the statement of my accused, which I have tried to convey literally, that psychologically he could not go through another trial, and we feel that this Chamber has all the elements necessary to correct any errors that may have been made by the First Instance Chamber. That is all that I wish to ask. I repeat again that this is against my will as a professional, just as during the testimony of the accused and when he was asked whether he pled guilty or not, I told him: "There is no evidence that you had committed the criminal offence. You should not plead guilty", but he said to me: "No, I cannot lie to the Yugoslav authorities. I cannot lie before this court. I cannot lie to anyone. It is my moral position that I must admit that this happened and it happened under the circumstances that I described". So he did not listen to me then. PRESIDENT CASSESE: Thank you. Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. Your Honour, the only submission I would wish to make at this stage is that --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: The only submission I would wish to make at this stage is that during the course of the sentencing hearing the Prosecutor expressed a view on appropriate penalties and said that a penalty of no more than ten years should be, in their submission, imposed. We wish to make no submissions on the issue of the penalty that is being suggested by the appellant today. PRESIDENT CASSESE: Thank you. I think that now the Appeals Chamber will retire and we will deliberate. So the hearing is adjourned. (3.45 pm)
